# oxframe 0.22.0

Text of this version of the documentation. Code samples are the fenced blocks from the pages.

Welcome to oxframe

  oxframe lets you make animations by writing code. You describe what happens, step by step, and
  oxframe turns it into a video — with a live editor to scrub through it and fine-tune the timing.

 Here is a whole animation: a square slides to the right and becomes a circle.

use oxframe::prelude::*;

#[oxframe::scene]
async fn intro(view: View)

fn main()

  If that reads like a recipe —  add a square, then move it and round its corners at the same time  — you already understand the main idea. The rest of these docs teach you the details, one small step
  at a time.

 How to read these docs

     Start here  gets oxframe running. If you just want to look around first, open
    the
     playground : it runs in your browser, nothing to install.

     Guide  is a series of short lessons. Each one adds a single idea and has a live preview
    you can play with. Read them in order — none of them assumes more than the lessons before it.

     Going further  is the reference: every node, effect, editor feature and command.

    Under the hood  explains how oxframe works inside, for the curious.

 What you need to know

  The basics of Rust are enough:  let , functions, and calling methods. You do not need
  to know
   async  — lesson 1 explains the only part of it you will use. No graphics experience required.

  Ready?  Install oxframe , or jump straight to
   lesson 1  in the browser.

3D scenes

  Lit 3D models inside a 2D animation: every position, rotation, color and the camera are signals,
  and the 3D view is a node like any other.

 A world and a view
 Turn on the  3d  feature of  oxframe :

oxframe =

let world = Scene3d::new();
let cube = world.add(Mesh::cube().color(Accent).roughness(0.35));
view.add(View3d::new(&world).size(640.0, 400.0));
cube.rotation().to(Vec3::new(0.0, 360.0, 0.0), 6.0).await;

   Scene3d::new()  is an empty world with a camera looking at the origin.
   scene.add(mesh)  puts a mesh in it and returns an  Object3d .
   View3d::new(&scene).size(640.0, 400.0)  shows the world in the 2D scene: it is a picture
  there, so position, opacity, effects, the 2D camera and layout work as for any node. Y is up and a cube
  is 1 unit wide.

 Meshes and materials

   Mesh::cube() ,  Mesh::sphere() ,  Mesh::plane()  (a floor facing
  up) and  Mesh::cylinder()  are 1 unit across.  Mesh::glb_file  reads a
  binary glTF model and fits it into the same 1-unit box; its base color is kept, textures are not
  read yet.
   Mesh::group()  draws nothing and holds children:  object.add(mesh)  adds one
  that moves, turns and scales with its parent.

  The material follows glTF:  .color()  takes a color or a theme role,
   .metallic()  goes from paint (0) to metal (1),  .roughness()  from mirror
  (0) to matte (1),  .emissive()  makes a surface glow and  .opacity()  makes
  it see-through.
   .position() ,  .rotation()  in degrees and  .scale()  place it.

 Everything is a signal

cube.position().to(Vec3::new(1.0, 0.0, 0.0), 1.0).await;
cube.color().to(Success, 0.5).await;
world.camera().position().to(Vec3::new(2.2, 1.8, 3.0), 2.0).await;
let sun = world.light(Light::directional((-2.0, -4.0, -1.0)));
sun.intensity().to(0.3, 1.0).await;

  An  Object3d  has position, rotation (degrees around X, then Y, then Z — animate past
  360 for more turns), orientation (a  Quat ), scale, color, metallic, roughness,
  emissive and opacity as signals.  scene.camera()  has position, target and field of
  view.
   scene.light(Light::directional(..))  adds sunlight and  Light::point(..)  a bulb;
  with no light added, a default sunlight gives each face of a box its own shade.

 2D labels on 3D points

let frame = view.add(View3d::new(&world).size(760.0, 520.0));
let to_view = frame.projector();
let label = frame.add(Txt::new().text("top").caption());
let (w, c) = (world.clone(), cube.clone());
label.x().bind(move || to_view(w.world_point(&c, Vec3::new(0.0, 0.5, 0.0))).x);

   view.projector()  maps a 3D point into the view's own coordinates, so a label or a
  leader line follows a corner while the model turns.  scene.world_point(object, point)  gives
  the point of an object after its parents' transforms.

 How it renders

  The renderer is a software rasterizer with a depth buffer and 2 × 2 supersampling for smooth
  edges. The same scene gives the same pixels in a render, in  oxframe check , in CI
  without a GPU and in the browser playground. A frame is redrawn only when something in the scene
  changed.
   .samples(1)  renders faster,  .resolution(2.0)  keeps the view sharp when it
  is scaled up. Shadows are not drawn yet.

  The same picture path is open to nodes of your own:  DrawCtx::image  draws a picture in
  a
   node you write .

Working with AI agents

  Coding agents like Claude Code, Codex or Cursor can write oxframe scenes for you. Every new
  project comes with instructions that teach them how — and a way for them to see what they made.

 What  oxframe init  adds

        AGENTS.md

        The project's rules for any agent: how scenes work, which commands to run, what never to do
        (non-deterministic code, editing  meta.json  by hand) and fixes for the most common
        compile errors.

        CLAUDE.md
       One line,  @AGENTS.md , so Claude Code reads the same file.

        .claude/skills/oxframe/

        A skill with a step-by-step workflow ( SKILL.md ) and an API cheat sheet ( reference.md ). Agents that support skills load it whenever you ask for a change to a scene.

 The files are plain Markdown. Read them, edit them, add your own project conventions.

 Letting the agent see its work

  Animation is visual, so compiling is not enough to know a change is right. The instructions tell
  the agent to look at the picture after every change:

oxframe check                 # storyboard.png + report.json; exit 1 on errors
# open out/check/storyboard.png and out/check/report.json, fix, run again
oxframe inspect --at 2.5      # scene tree at that time, when a frame looks wrong

  The storyboard is a grid of frames with the time under each cell. The report names the rule, the
  node and the source line.  oxframe snapshot  is still there for one full-size still.
  Nothing keeps running —  oxframe dev  is for you, not for the agent.

     out/check/storyboard.png  of a scene with a mistake: the list sits on top of the title.

 A good way to work together

   Keep  oxframe dev  open in your browser.

    Ask the agent for a change in plain words:  "after the title, slide three cards in from the left, one after another" .

    The agent edits the code and checks it with  oxframe check ; your preview reloads by
    itself.

    Fine-tune timing yourself with markers and sliders. The agent is told to keep your
     meta.json  values, so your adjustments survive its next edit.

 Keeping the files up to date
 After upgrading oxframe, refresh the instructions:

oxframe agents          # refreshes the generated files
oxframe agents --force  # also replaces files you made your own

  Generated files carry an  oxframe-agents  marker comment. To keep your own version of a file,
  delete that comment — files without it are left alone. Projects created with an older CLI can get the
  files the same way.

 Connecting an MCP client

   oxframe mcp  speaks MCP over stdin and stdout. Point Claude Code, or any other client,
  at that command with the project directory as its working directory. The tools are
   check ,  storyboard ,  render_frame ,  inspect ,
   render_graph ,  list_components ,  docs_search  and
   render .  docs_search  looks through the docs of the CLI's own version.
   render_graph  lists the render passes at one time, so an agent can see that a
   lens_drops  or a  ripple  runs, or why  check  reports
   input_cycle .

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "oxframe":
  }
}

  Every command also takes  --json  and then prints a single JSON object on stdout. A
  compile error includes the compiler text and a  hints  array for the mistakes agents
  make most often (a forgotten  .await , a builder never passed to  add , a
  theme token used as a number, and the rest).

 For tools that read the web

  Each docs version has a plain-text index and a full dump, generated from the pages when the site
  is built. The current version is   /llms.txt   and
    /llms-full.txt  . A pinned version is
   /docs/<series>/llms.txt  (for example
    /docs/0.1/llms.txt  ). The current series redirects to
  the unversioned files, so a link written for today's version keeps working after that series is
  archived.

Camera

  A camera zooms, pans and turns the view of everything added to it. Show a whole diagram, move in
  on one detail, follow something as it travels — while titles stay put.

 World and screen

  Add a  Camera  to the view and build the world inside it. Everything you add to the camera
  is seen through it; everything you add to the view itself stays on screen, which is where titles, captions
  and labels belong.

let cam = view.add(Camera::new());
let diagram = cam.add(Group::new());      // the world: seen through the camera
diagram.add(Rect::new().width(360.0).height(160.0));
view.add(Txt::new().text("Title").h2().to_edge(Edge::Top)); // on screen

 Moving the camera

  A camera has four signals, animated like any other property:  x  and
   y  are the point it looks at,  zoom  is how close it is (2 = twice as big),
  and  rotation  turns the view (in degrees, clockwise).

cam.fit(diagram, 120.0, 0.0).await;   // all of it in the frame, 120 px to spare
cam.center_on(api, 1.0).await;         // bring one node to the middle
cam.zoom().to(2.5, 1.0).await;         // move in
cam.rotation().to(15.0, 1.0).await;    // tilt
cam.reset(1.2).await;                  // back to x = y = 0, zoom 1, no rotation

   fit  measures the node when it is called, so a layout that has grown is framed at its
  current size. A duration of  0.0  jumps there at once — handy for the first frame. To
  move and zoom together, run both in  all :

  all((cam.center_on(api, 1.2), cam.zoom().to(1.6, 1.2))).await;

 Following a node

  Bind the camera's position to a node and it follows it every frame. The next animation of the
  camera's  x  or  y  releases it.

let (px, py) = (packet.x(), packet.y());
cam.x().bind(move || px.get());
cam.y().bind(move || py.get());
packet.x().to(900.0, 2.0).await;       // the camera rides along
cam.fit(diagram, 120.0, 1.4).await;    // and lets go here

 Sharp at any zoom

  Nothing is stretched: every frame is drawn again at its final scale. Text and outlines stay crisp
  at ×10, and blurs, shadows and glows grow with the zoom instead of turning to mush — on the GPU
  and the CPU renderer alike.

 Checking

    oxframe check   does not report nodes inside a camera as out
  of frame: when you zoom in on a detail, the rest of the world is supposed to be outside. Text overlap
  and contrast are still checked, and nodes added to the view are checked as usual.

Animated charts and plots

  Axes, number lines, function plots and bars. Data coordinates map into a box, and every part
  follows when a range animates.

 Axes

   Axes::new()  is a plotting box with a grid, two axes with arrows, ticks and labels.
   .x_range(-5.0..5.0)  and  .y_range(-2.0..2.0)  set the data ranges;
   .width()  and  .height()  set the box in pixels or  pct()  of
  the frame (80 % by 60 % by default);  .no_grid()  drops the grid. The axes cross at 0 when
  0 is in range. Lines and labels take their colors from the theme.

let axes = view.add(Axes::new().x_range(-5.0..5.0).y_range(-2.0..2.0));
axes.x_range().to(-10.0..10.0, 1.0).await;

   axes.x_range()  is a signal of  Interval , so
   axes.x_range().to(-10.0..10.0, 1.0)  zooms out. Ticks sit on round steps (1, 2 or 5 times
  a power of ten), and each label keeps its value while the range slides, so nothing flickers.

 Function plots

   axes.plot(|x| x.sin())  draws a function and returns a  Plot . It is
  sampled again every frame, finer where it bends, so it follows the ranges. It breaks where it
  jumps —  tan  has no vertical line across its gaps — and it is cut at the edge of the
  box.  .stroke(Accent)  and  .width(4.0)  style it,  .draw_on()
  draws it like any path, and  plot.to_fn(|x| x.cos(), 1.0)  morphs it: every x moves from
  the old value to the new one.

let wave = axes.plot(|x| x.sin()).stroke(Accent);
wave.draw_on().await;
let x = Signal::new(-5.0);
axes.point_on(&wave, x.clone());
x.to(5.0, 2.0).await;
wave.to_fn(|x| (2.0 * x).sin(), 1.0).await;

   axes.point_on(&plot, x)  keeps a dot on the curve at a signal  x .
   axes.c2p(x, y)  gives the scene point of a data point, and
   axes.place(node, x, y)  keeps any node there while the ranges move.

 Bars and data

   axes.bars([3.0, 7.5])  draws a bar per value at x = 0, 1, 2… with the value above it;
  set the x range to  -0.5..n - 0.5 . With bars the y axis sits at the left edge.
   bars.value(0).to(9.0, 1.0)  grows one bar and its label, and
   .labels(["a", "b"])  names the bars.  axes.line_series(..)  draws a line
  through data points and  axes.scatter(..)  a dot per point.

let bars = axes.bars([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]).labels(["rustc", "gcc", "clang"]);
stagger(0.15, [3.2, 7.5, 5.1].into_iter().enumerate(), |(i, v)| bars.value(i).to(v, 1.0)).await;

 Number lines

   NumberLine::new(0.0..10.0)  is a single axis with ticks, labels and an arrow. It has
  the same methods as the axes:  x_range ,  c2p  and  place .

  There is no pie chart yet; draw slices with  Custom . Long rows of a
   BulletList  now wrap inside the frame, so a list of results next to a chart stays readable.

Check rules

  What each rule in an  oxframe check  report means and how to fix it. Every issue in
   report.json  links to its section here in its  docs  field (Rust code gets
  the same link from  Issue::docs ).

   oxframe check  plays every scene, samples frames and reports what a viewer would see
  as a mistake. An error makes the command exit 1; a warning does not. Each issue names the rule,
  the time range, the node and the line of code that added it. Thresholds live in
   oxframe.toml  under  [check] .

  An issue on a node comes with a close-up in  out/check/issues/ : the frame around the
  node at full resolution, the node outlined in red. Its path is the issue's  crop  field
  in  report.json , next to  bounds , the node's box. A node wholly outside
  the frame gets the strip along the edge it went past.

     issues/02-out_of_frame.png : a headline that runs off the right edge.

         Before:

         After:

 Frame and layout

  out_of_frame

  A node stays outside the frame (error) or outside the safe area near the edges (warning). A node
  that only passes through the edge, entering or leaving, is not reported.

  Fix: move it inward, make it smaller, or place it with  pct() ,
   to_edge(Edge::…)  or a  Layout .  --safe-inset 0  turns the warning
  off for a frame without a safe area.

  text_overflow

  Text is wider than its block: its  max_width , or the  Layout  that holds it.

  Fix: shorter text, a smaller type style ( .h2() ,  .body() ), or a wider
  block.

  text_overlap
 Two pieces of text cover each other.

  Fix: place one relative to the other ( next_to(other, Side::Bottom) ), put both in a
   Layout , or fade the first out before the second comes in.

  covers_text
 A shader is drawn over text, so the text is hidden behind it.

 Fix: add the shader before the text, or move the text out of its box.

  low_contrast

  Text is too close in color to what is behind it, below the WCAG ratio (4.5 by default,
   --min-contrast ).

  Fix: use theme roles, which are built to contrast:  Text  on  Background  or
   Surface ,  OnAccent  on  Accent .

 Timing

  too_fast

  Text is not on screen long enough to read at the reading speed ( --chars-per-second ),
  or a large move is quicker than  --min-motion .

  Fix: hold the text with  wait_for(…)  after it appears, or give the move a longer
  duration. In a presentation, hold before each  slide_break : the video plays through
  it.

  dead_time

  Nothing changes on screen for longer than  --max-still  (not checked with a soundtrack).

 Fix: shorten the wait, or give the viewer something to look at while it lasts.

 Voice

  voice_cut
 A spoken line runs past the end of its scene and is cut.
 Fix:  line.await  before the scene ends, or shorten the line.

  voice_overlap
 Two spoken lines overlap.
 Fix: start the second line after  first.await .

 Shaders

  shader_error

  The WGSL of a shader does not compile, or a name or type does not match its  Params .

  Fix: the message names the line in the shader; see  lesson 13 .

  param_unknown
 A parameter is set from Rust that the shader's  Params  does not have.
 Fix: add it to  struct Params  or correct the name.

  shader_slow
 A shader takes longer per frame than the budget.
 Fix: a smaller box, fewer loop iterations, or a preset from  shaders:: .

  input_cycle

  A shader that reads drawn pixels ( lens_drops , an effect) is inside a group that is
  itself drawn as a layer (opacity below 1, blur, clip, blend, shadow, another effect). The shader
  is skipped.

 Fix: put the effect on that group instead, or take the node out of it.

 Determinism and media

  nondeterministic
 Two paints of the same frame differ, so a seek or a render would not match the preview.

  Fix: draw only from signals and  ctx.time() ; take randomness from
   ctx.rng(seed)  or  random() , never from the clock.

  video_unavailable
 A video clip cannot be opened; it shows as a dark box.

  Fix: check the path, build with the  video  feature and install ffmpeg. The playground cannot
  play videos.

CLI reference

  Everything the  oxframe  command can do. You will use  dev  most of the time;
  the rest are for creating, checking and exporting.

 The everyday loop

oxframe init my-video     # once: create a project
cd my-video
oxframe dev               # edit code, watch the preview update
oxframe render            # when you are happy: out/my-video.mp4

 Commands

  Every command accepts  --json . It then prints one JSON object on stdout ( ok ,  exit , and on failure  error ,  diagnostics  and
   hints ) and keeps the log on stderr.

  oxframe init <name>

  Creates a folder with a ready-to-run project:  Cargo.toml  (SDK version pinned),
   src/main.rs  with one scene, its  meta.json ,  oxframe.toml ,
   .gitignore  and instructions for AI coding agents (see
   Working with AI agents ).
   --template node  makes a library crate with a node of your own instead (see
   Writing your own node ).

       --sdk-path <dir>   Use a local  oxframe-sdk  checkout instead of crates.io (also
         OXFRAME_SDK_PATH ).

  oxframe dev

  Builds the project, opens the editor in your browser and rebuilds every time you save. If the code
  does not compile, the error shows over the preview and the last good build keeps playing.

       --port <n>   Editor port (default 3000).
       --open  /  --no-open   Open the browser, or don't (overrides  oxframe.toml ).
       --release   Optimized build: slower to compile, faster to play heavy scenes.
       --gpu   Draw the preview on the GPU (vello). The CPU is the default;  --cpu  is still accepted.

  oxframe present

  Builds the project like  oxframe dev  and opens it as a presentation: full screen,
  stopping at every  slide_break  and scene end. N opens the speaker notes. Takes
   --port ,  --no-open ,  --release  and  --gpu . See
   Presentations from scenes .

  oxframe snapshot --at <seconds>

  Renders single frames as PNG without ffmpeg — handy to check a moment in the animation, to put a
  still in a README, or for an AI agent to look at its own work.

oxframe snapshot --at 1.5                       # out/snapshots/ -1.50.png
oxframe snapshot --at 0 --at 2 --at 4           # three frames
oxframe snapshot --at 1 --out cover.png         # exactly this file
oxframe snapshot --at 0.5 --scene outro         # time from the start of a scene

  Each written file is printed on its own line ( path frame=N t=T ), so scripts can pick
  them up. Default size is 960×540; change it with  --size 1920x1080 .

  oxframe render

  Builds in release mode and renders a video. See  Rendering video  for examples.

       --out <path>   Output file or folder (default  out/<project>.mp4 ).
       --format <f>    mp4 ,  webm ,  prores  or  png ; by default
        taken from the  --out  extension.
       --scene <name>   Only this scene.
       --range a..b   Only this time range, in seconds; either side can be left out ( 2.. ).
       --size WxH   Output size, e.g.  3840x2160 .
       --aspect <shape>    16:9 ,  9:16 ,  1:1 , or  all .
         all  writes one file per format declared with
         Project::aspects .
       --gpu   Draw on the GPU (vello). The CPU (tiny-skia) is the default: faster here and byte-for-byte
        deterministic.  --cpu  is still accepted and wins.
       --no-audio   Leave the soundtrack out.

  oxframe check

  Compiles the project ( cargo check ), validates every  meta.json , compares
  the versions of the CLI, SDK and editor, and then looks at the picture. It writes
   out/check/storyboard.png  (a grid of frames at markers and at equal intervals, with
  the time and marker name under each cell) and  out/check/report.json .

  Each issue has a rule, a severity ( error  or  warning ), a time range, the
  node name, the source  file:line  and a hint:

     out_of_frame  — a node stays outside the frame (or inside the frame but outside the safe
    area, which is a warning).

    text_overlap  — two text blocks cover each other.

     text_overflow  — text is wider than its  max_width  or its layout parent.

    low_contrast  — text against its backdrop is below WCAG 4.5:1.

     too_fast  — a long line flashes too briefly to read (error), or a large move is shorter
    than 0.15s (warning).

     dead_time  — nothing on screen changes for several seconds and the project has no soundtrack
    (warning).

     nondeterministic  — painting the same frame twice did not match. Draw from the time
    and  ctx.rng(seed) , not from a counter saved in the closure.

  Errors make the command exit 1; warnings do not. A project that declares
   Project::aspects  is checked in every format; the other storyboards are
   storyboard-9x16.png  and  storyboard-1x1.png .  --frames  also
  writes each cell at full size under  out/check/frames/ . The check renders only the
  frames it needs, on the CPU, at a reduced size, so a 30 second scene finishes in a few seconds.

  An issue on a node also gets a close-up:  out/check/issues/01-out_of_frame.png  and so
  on, that part of the frame at full resolution with the node outlined in red (up to 24 per check).
  In  report.json  the issue then has  bounds , the node's box at the start of
  the issue in scene units (as in  oxframe inspect ), and  crop , the path of
  the picture relative to  out/check/ . An agent opens the crop instead of hunting for
  the problem on the storyboard.

  The report also lists  motion : every node that travels, with its
   file:line , the stretches of time it visibly moves ( moves , in seconds),
  where it starts and ends, and the length of its path. Read it to check timing without watching the
  video.  out/check/trajectories/<scene>.png  draws those paths over the scene's
  last frame, numbered as in  motion . A hard cut between scenes shows on the storyboard
  as the last frame of one scene next to the first frame of the next.

  To see what an edit changed, keep the frames from before it and compare with
   oxframe check --against <dir> :

oxframe check --frames --out out/before
# edit the scene
oxframe check --against out/before

  Each frame that changed is listed with the share of its pixels that moved, and
   out/check/diff/  holds the frame dimmed with the changed pixels in red. The report
  gets a  comparison : changed, unchanged, added and removed frames. An edit that changed
  frames it should not have shows up at once. The reference frames are read with
   Image::decode_png .

  Name a node with  .name("title")  so the report is readable. Without a name it is
  labeled by the line that called  add .

  oxframe inspect --at <seconds>

  Prints the scene tree at that time as JSON: kind, name, source location, scene bounds, opacity,
  text and draw order.  --scene outro  measures the time from the start of that scene.
   --graph  adds a  passes  array: one vector pass, then a composite for each layer
  (a group opacity, a blend, a blur, a shadow or a clip). Without the flag the JSON is unchanged.

  oxframe add <block>

  Copies a ready-made, checked block into  src/blocks/  and adds
   mod blocks;  to  src/main.rs . Each block is one call that plays itself in
  and returns its group:  blocks::stat_counter(view, 1280.0, "stars").await . With no
  name it lists them:  logo-reveal ,  stat-counter ,
   progress-bar ,  quote-card ,  before-after ,
   timeline . The copied file is yours to edit;  --force  replaces it.

  oxframe doctor

  Checks what building and rendering need — Rust 1.95 or newer, a C linker, ffmpeg, and inside a
  project whether it is on the SDK your CLI makes — and prints the fix for each missing piece on
  your system. Exits 2 when something required is missing.

  oxframe agents

  Writes or refreshes  AGENTS.md ,  CLAUDE.md  and
   .claude/skills/oxframe/  — run it after upgrading oxframe. Files you edited yourself
  are left alone unless you pass  --force .

  oxframe upgrade

  Moves the project to the SDK version your CLI is made for: updates the  oxframe  pin in
   Cargo.toml  (keeping your formatting), runs  cargo update  and refreshes the
  agent files. If the project already uses a newer SDK, it tells you to update the CLI instead.

  oxframe mcp

  An MCP server on stdin and stdout, for Claude Code and other clients. Started in a project, it
  serves  check ,  storyboard ,  render_frame ,
   inspect ,  render_graph ,
   list_components ,  docs_search  and  render .
   render_graph  is  oxframe inspect --graph  without the node tree: the
  render passes at one time, with the shader of each effect pass. Messages are newline-delimited
  JSON-RPC; a  Content-Length  frame is accepted too. Nothing but the protocol is written to
  stdout.

 Updating

cargo install oxframe-cli --force   # a new CLI
oxframe upgrade                     # then in each project

  Projects pin the SDK version, so a release never changes an existing project on its own. Once a
  day the CLI checks crates.io in the background and mentions a newer version; set
   OXFRAME_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1  to turn that off.

 oxframe.toml
 Project settings for the CLI. Every key is optional.

[dev]
port = 3000
open = true        # open the browser on "oxframe dev"
profile = "dev"    # or "release"

[render]
ffmpeg = "/opt/ffmpeg/bin/ffmpeg"   # default: ffmpeg from PATH

[theme]
name = "dark"         # dark, light, midnight, paper, vivid
accent = "#68abdf"    # one brand color; other colors stay readable

[check]
interval = 1.0        # seconds between storyboard frames
safe_inset = 48       # px; 0 turns the safe-area warning off
min_contrast = 4.5
min_motion = 0.15
max_still = 3.0
chars_per_second = 20
min_chars = 24
cell_width = 320

 Exit codes

      0  Success.
      1  Your code does not compile, the scene fails, or  oxframe check  found an error.
      2  Environment: no ffmpeg, port in use, cannot write a file.
      3  Version mismatch between the CLI, SDK and editor.

 Add  -v  to any command for detailed logs.

 Security

  The editor server listens on 127.0.0.1 only, checks the  Origin  of every WebSocket connection
  and requires a one-time token. The CLI runs nothing but cargo and your own project.

Writing your own node

  A struct that draws itself becomes a node: animatable fields, layout, effects and checks, like the
  built-in ones.

 A struct that draws

  Turn on the  unstable-node-api  feature of  oxframe . The API may change
  until it has outside users.

oxframe =

#[derive(Node)]
pub struct Gauge

impl Draw for Gauge {
    fn draw(&self, ctx: &mut DrawCtx)
    fn size(&self) -> (f64, f64)
}

   #[derive(Node)]  on a struct that implements  Draw  makes it a node. Each
  field marked  #[signal]  gets a setter on the builder,  Gauge::new() , and a
  signal on the handle,  GaugeHandle , so  gauge.value().to(0.8, 1.0)
  animates it. Fields without the mark are set once on the builder. Every field type needs
   Default  and  Clone .

let gauge = view.add(Gauge::new().size(240.0));
gauge.value().to(0.8, 1.0).await;

 Drawing

   Draw::draw  paints with the same  DrawCtx  as  Custom :
   ctx.line ,  ctx.circle ,  ctx.rect ,  ctx.path  and
   DrawCtx::arc  for gauges and rings, each followed by  .fill(..)  or
   .stroke(.., width)  with a color or a theme role. Coordinates are the node's own, with the
  origin at the center of its box.

  Draw only from the fields and  ctx.time() , and take randomness from
   ctx.rng(seed) . The frame is painted again on every seek, and
   oxframe check  reports a node whose two paints of one frame differ.

 Its box

   Draw::size  gives the box that flex layout,  Camera::fit  and
   oxframe check  use; the default is 100 by 100. Everything else comes with the node:
  position, rotation, scale, opacity, relative placement such as  to_edge , effects, flex
  properties and theme colors.  check  and  inspect  name it by its type, so
  an issue reads  Gauge , not  Custom .

 A crate of your own
  oxframe init --template node my-node

   oxframe init --template node my-node  makes a library crate: the node in
   src/lib.rs , a demo scene in  examples/demo.rs
  ( cargo run --example demo -- render ) and a reference test that renders the node on
  the CPU and checks its pixels. Publish it like any crate; scenes add it as a dependency.

 The playground has the feature on, so a node written in a scene there works too.

The editor

  A tour of the editor. It is the same app under  oxframe dev  on your machine and in the playground
  on this site.

    The viewport, the inspector on the right and the timeline below, on the project  oxframe init  creates.

 The four areas

   Viewport

    The current frame. Scroll to zoom around the cursor, hold  Alt  (or the middle button) and
    drag to pan, double-click to fit. Click a node to select it.

   Timeline

    Play, pause and scrub. Shows scene boundaries, markers and the soundtrack's waveform. Drag a
    marker to retime everything that waits for it.

   Inspector

    The node tree, the live values of the selected node's signals, sliders for  tune!
    values and the list of named eases.

   Curve editor

    Opens when you click an ease. Drag the two handles or pick a preset; a dot previews the motion.

 When code does not compile

  The compiler's message appears over the viewport with the file and line. The last build that
  worked keeps playing, so you never lose your place. Fix the code and save — the error goes away by
  itself.

 Shortcuts

       Space   Play / pause
       ←   →   Previous / next frame
       Shift + ←   →   Jump 10 frames
       Home   End   Start / end
       M   Move the selected marker to the playhead
       Esc   Close dialogs, dismiss errors

 Small conveniences

    The frame, zoom and selection are kept in the URL — a reload or rebuild returns you to the same
    spot.

   Several browser tabs can be connected to one  oxframe dev  at the same time.
   In the playground,  Share  puts the whole source into the link.

Effects

  Gradients, dashes, shadows, blur, blend modes and clipping. Every effect is a signal, so it
  animates like any other property —  .to() ,  .ease()  and
   .bind()
  all work.

 Paint

Rect::new()
    .fill_gradient(Gradient::linear((-100.0, 0.0), (100.0, 0.0)).stops([color!("#e13238"), color!("#f5c242")]))
    .stroke(Color::WHITE).line_width(4.0)
    .dash(vec![12.0, 8.0])          // animate dash_offset for marching ants
    .line_cap(LineCap::Butt)

  Gradients are in the node's own coordinates (origin at its center).  Gradient::radial(center, radius)  works the same way. Two gradients with the same number of stops interpolate.

 Layers

  A node is drawn into its own layer when its effect must apply to the node and its children as a
  whole: group opacity (overlaps do not get darker), blend modes, blur and shadows. Plain shapes
  skip the layer and stay fast.

Group::new().opacity(0.5)                         // group opacity
Circle::new().clip(true)                         // children added to it are clipped to the circle
Circle::new().blend(BlendMode::Multiply)         // Multiply, Screen, Overlay, …
Txt::new().blur(12.0)                            // Gaussian blur (σ, node units)
Rect::new().shadow(Color::BLACK.with_alpha(0.6), 16.0, (0.0, 12.0))
Circle::new().glow(color!("#68abdf"), 20.0)      // shadow without offset

 Order and pivot

Rect::new().z_index(-1.0)            // drawn below its siblings
Rect::new().anchor((-1.0, -1.0))     // (x, y) is the top-left corner and the rotation pivot

  Blur and shadows are rasterized by the same code on both renderers (tiny-skia), so CPU and GPU
  output match; only the area a layer can touch is processed.

Formulas

  Math typeset by Typst, as nodes you color and animate glyph by glyph. The font is bundled, so no
  TeX install is needed and a formula looks the same on every machine.

    The last frame of the
      formulas  example on GitHub .

 Turn on the math feature

oxframe =

  The feature adds the Typst compiler and a 1.4 MB font to your binary, so it is off by default. It
  works with  oxframe dev ,  oxframe check  and  oxframe render
  on your machine and in CI. The browser playground does not have it: the playground's engine stays small,
  so formulas cannot be tried there.

 A formula by its source

let euler = view.add(Math::new("e^(i pi) + 1 = 0").size(140.0));
stagger(0.08, euler.paths(), |glyph| glyph.pop_in()).await;
euler.color().to(Accent, 0.6).await;

let sum = view.add(
    Math::new("sum_(k=1)^n k = (n(n + 1)) / 2")
        .display()
        .size(72.0)
        .y(220.0),
);
sum.fade_in().await;

   Math::new("e^(i pi) + 1 = 0")  takes
   Typst math syntax  without the dollar signs. A formula
  Typst cannot set (an unknown symbol, a missing bracket) stops the scene with Typst's message, which
  names the formula.

     You write  You get

       x^2 ,  x_i   superscript, subscript
       (a + b) / c   a fraction
       sqrt(x)   a square root
       sum_(k=1)^n ,  integral_0^1   sums and integrals with limits
       alpha pi   Greek letters by name
       vec(1, 2) ,  mat(1, 2; 3, 4)   a vector, a matrix
       "text"   upright words inside a formula

 Size, color and display style

   .size(px)  is the font size in pixels, as for  Txt ; the box is as tall as
  a line of text, so formulas of one size line up.  .color(..)  takes a color or a theme
  role and defaults to the theme's text color.  .display()  sets the formula on its own
  line, as  $ … $  does in Typst: a sum gets its limits above and below and a fraction is full
  size. Without it the formula is set inline, as in running text.

 Animate it

  The handle,  Math , is a node like any other:  fade_in ,
   next_to ,  scale  and layout work on it.  color()  is a signal
  for the whole formula, and  paths()  gives every glyph and rule (fraction bars, root
  signs) in reading order, for  stagger . Glyphs are filled shapes, so write them on with
   pop_in  or  fade_in  rather than  draw_on .

 Run the example from a clone of the SDK:
  cargo run -p oxframe-examples --features math --bin formulas -- preview

Install and first project
 Five minutes from nothing to an editor with your own animation in it.

   Want to skip installing?  Everything in the guide also works in the
   playground . Come back here when you want to render videos on your
  machine.

 1. Install the tools
 You need Rust with a C linker and, to make videos, ffmpeg.

# Rust (skip if you have it)
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh

# a C linker, if this machine has never built C or Rust
sudo apt install build-essential   # Debian/Ubuntu
xcode-select --install             # macOS

# ffmpeg
sudo apt install ffmpeg        # Linux
brew install ffmpeg            # macOS
winget install Gyan.FFmpeg     # Windows

# the oxframe command, prebuilt: seconds, checksum-verified
curl -fsSL https://github.com/oxygenframe/oxframe-cli/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh   # Linux, macOS
# Windows (PowerShell):
#   powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -c "irm https://github.com/oxygenframe/oxframe-cli/releases/latest/download/install.ps1 | iex"
# or with cargo: cargo binstall oxframe-cli (prebuilt), cargo install oxframe-cli (from source)

  The installer puts  oxframe  in  ~/.local/bin
  ( %LOCALAPPDATA%\oxframe\bin  on Windows, added to your  PATH ); set
   OXFRAME_INSTALL_DIR  to change that. Rust is still needed either way: your scenes are
  Rust code.  oxframe doctor  then checks that everything a build needs is there.

 Requirements

      System  Linux (x86_64, arm64), macOS (Intel, Apple Silicon), Windows (x86_64).
      Rust  1.95 or newer, from  rustup .  rustup update  moves
        an older one forward.
      C linker  Rust links programs with it. Linux:  build-essential  (Debian, Ubuntu),
         gcc  (Fedora),  base-devel  (Arch). macOS: the Xcode command line tools.
        Windows: the MSVC build tools, which rustup offers to install.
      ffmpeg  For MP4, WebM and ProRes. The editor,  oxframe check , snapshots and PNG frames
        work without it.
      GPU  Not needed: frames are drawn on the CPU.  --gpu  uses Vulkan, Metal or DirectX 12
        when the machine has them.
      Disk  A few GB per project for Rust's build cache in  target/ ; the first build fills
        it.

 2. Create a project

oxframe init hello
cd hello
oxframe dev --open

  The first build takes a minute or two — Rust compiles the engine once. Then your browser opens the
  editor: the animation in the middle, the timeline at the bottom. Press  Space  to play.

   The new project in  oxframe dev , with the text node selected.

 3. Change something

  Open  src/main.rs , find  color!("#68abdf")  and change it to
   color!("#2ecc71") . Save. About a second later the editor shows the new color — and
  stays on the same frame. That loop, edit → save → look, is how you will work.

 4. Make a video
  oxframe render        # writes out/hello.mp4

 What is in the project

       src/main.rs   Your scene. Everything you write goes here.
       src/intro.meta.json   Timing values you adjust in the editor (lesson 7). Commit it.
       oxframe.toml   Settings for  oxframe dev  and  render .
       assets/   Images and audio.
       AGENTS.md ,  .claude/   Instructions for AI coding assistants (see  Working with AI agents ).

  Next,  lesson 1  walks through that first scene line by line.

14. Charts and graphs

  A function on a set of axes, a dot that rides it, and a zoom that the whole chart follows.

 Axes map data into a box

   Axes::new().x_range(-4.0..4.0).y_range(-1.5..1.5)  puts data coordinates into a box with
  a grid, ticks and labels. You think in data — x from -4 to 4 — and oxframe finds the pixels.

 A plot is a function of x

   axes.plot(|x| (x * 1.5).sin())  draws the curve. It is a path, so
   .draw_on()  works as in lesson 9.  axes.point_on(&curve, x)  keeps a dot on
  it; move the signal  x  and the dot rides the curve.

 Everything follows the ranges

   curve.to_fn(..)  morphs into another function, and
   axes.x_range().to(-8.0..8.0, 1.0)  zooms out: the grid, the labels, the curve and the dot
  move together, because they are drawn from the range every frame.

     Plot  |x| x.tan()  and look at the gaps.
     Add bars:  axes.bars([1.0, 0.5]).labels(["a", "b"]) .

      Axes  maps data into a box; ranges are signals.

       plot ,  point_on  and  to_fn  draw and move functions.

       Animated charts and plots  has bars, data series and number lines.

Components

  An explainer is a handful of blocks. Each one takes its color and type from the theme, places
  itself, and answers  enter ,  next  and  exit . The player is the
  gallery example; the still under each block is the moment that block is on screen.

 Title card

let title = view.add(TitleCard::new("Binary search").subtitle("O(log n)"));
title.enter().await;
title.next().await;
title.exit().await;

  enter  fades the card and the title in.  next  reveals the subtitle.

 Chapter marker

let chapter = view.add(ChapterMarker::new("1  Search"));
chapter.enter().await;

 A label pinned to the top safe area, including on a vertical frame.

 Bullet list

let steps = view.add(BulletList::new(["Take the middle", "Compare", "Drop half"]));
steps.enter().await;
for _ in 0..steps.len()

  enter  shows the stack. Each  next  reveals one row.

 Code explainer

let code = view.add(
    CodeExplainer::new("lo + (hi - lo) / 2").step(1, 1, "the middle"),
);
code.enter().await;
code.next().await;

   enter  shows the source. Each  next  focuses the next line range (1-based, inclusive)
  and sets the caption. A light theme uses a light code theme.

 Flow diagram

let flow = view.add(FlowDiagram::new().edge("Client", "API").edge("API", "DB"));
flow.enter().await;
for _ in 0..flow.len()

  You name the links. The diagram lays the nodes out in layers, left to right.
   .down()  stacks the layers.  next  highlights the next node.

 Callout

let card = view.add(Rect::new().size(280.0).fill(Surface));
let call = view.add(Callout::new(card).text("the middle"));
call.enter().await;
call.next().await;

  The caption sits above the target.  enter  draws the arrow,  next  shows the words.

 Lower third

let lower = view.add(LowerThird::new("Ada").role("walks the half"));
lower.enter().await;
lower.next().await;

 Pinned to the bottom safe area.  next  reveals the role.

 End card

let end = view.add(EndCard::new("That's the search").note("Repeat from the top"));
end.enter().await;
end.next().await;
end.exit().await;

 Same rhythm as a title card. The note waits for  next .

  The gallery example  components  is a full explainer in under 40 lines.
   Project::aspects  makes  oxframe check  look at 16:9, 9:16 and 1:1.

9. Drawing and morphing
 Draw an outline as if with a pen, then turn one shape into another.

 Drawing an outline on

  Every outline has two properties,  start  and  end , that say which part of
  it is drawn — as a fraction of its length.  .end(0.0)  hides it; animating
   end
  to 1 draws it on. Animating
   start  to 1 afterwards erases it from the beginning.

 Paths and morphing

  A  Path  is any shape you can describe with lines and curves — usually written in SVG
  path syntax ( "M0 -150 L44 -46 ..." ), which every vector tool can export. Animating
   data  to another path morphs between them. oxframe lines up the two outlines first, so a
  star turns into a heart without twisting.

  shape.data().to(heart, 1.2).await;

     Morph back to the star at the end.
     Animate  start  to 1 to erase the outline.

      start / end  control how much of an outline is drawn.
      Path  +  data().to(other_path)  morphs shapes.

4. Easing
 Why some animations feel natural and others feel robotic — and how to choose.

  All three balls travel the same distance in the same time. The difference is  easing : how the speed changes along the way.

    LINEAR  moves at a constant speed. It looks mechanical.

    The  default  starts slowly, speeds up, and settles in. Real objects move like this,
    which is why it is the default.

     OUT_BACK  overshoots a little and comes back — playful, good for things popping in.

  ball.x().to(500.0, 1.5).ease(presets::OUT_BACK).await;

   presets  has the common curves ( IN_OUT_CUBIC ,  OUT_EXPO ,
   IN_OUT_SINE , …). There are also bouncy ones:  .ease(oxframe::bounce_out)
  and  .ease(oxframe::elastic_out) .

     Try  presets::IN_OUT_EXPO  on the middle ball.
     Give the last ball  oxframe::bounce_out .

       .ease(...)  after  .to(...)  picks the curve; the default is a smooth in-and-out.

     In lesson 7 you will edit curves visually instead of picking presets.

7. Tweak timing in the editor

  Some things are easier to adjust by eye than by number. oxframe lets you do that without touching
  code.

  When an animation should start "on the beat" or a size "looks right", guessing numbers and
  recompiling is slow. These three helpers move the decision into the editor:

       wait_until("go").await   A  marker  on the timeline. Drag it, and everything after it moves.
       tune!("size", 160.0)   A number with a  slider  in the inspector; 160 is the starting value.
       .ease(ease!("move"))   An easing curve you shape in the  curve editor .

 Where the values live

  The first time your scene runs, oxframe writes these names and their starting values into a file
  next to your code,
   src/<scene>.meta.json . From then on the file wins: the editor changes the file,
  the code only provides defaults. Commit the file — it is part of your animation.

{
  "eases":  ,
  "markers":  ,
  "tunables":  ,
  "version": 1
}

      Open the lesson in the playground. Drag the  go  marker to the right on the timeline.

     Move the  size  slider in the inspector.
     Click the  move  ease in the inspector and bend the curve.

     Markers, tunables and named eases are values you adjust in the editor.
     They are saved in  meta.json ; the code only sets defaults.

6. Groups and layout
 Put shapes inside other shapes, and let a layout arrange them for you.

 Children

  So far everything was added to the  view . You can also add shapes to other shapes:
   sun.add(...) . A child's position is measured from its parent, and it moves, rotates
  and fades along with it. Rotate the sun, and the planet orbits; rotate the planet, and its moon
  orbits the planet.

  Group  is a shape that draws nothing — a container for others.

 Layout

  Placing ten cards by hand is tedious. A  Layout  places its children in a row (or
   .column() ), with  .gap()  between them and  .padding()  around.
  It works like flexbox on the web: children can  .grow(1.0)  to fill space, the row can
   .wrap(true) , and
   .grid(3)  makes a three-column grid.

  Layout settings are animatable like everything else. Animate the gap and the cards slide apart;
  remove a card and the others close the gap.

     Add  .width(500.0)  to the row and  .grow(1.0)  to one card.
     Add a second moon to the planet.

      parent.add(child)  — children follow their parent.
      Layout  arranges children: row, column, wrap, grid, grow.

1. Your first animation

  You will add a circle to the screen and move it. That is most of what animation code ever does.

 A scene is a function

  An animation in oxframe is called a  scene , and a scene is just a function marked
  with
   #[oxframe::scene] . It receives the  view  — the canvas you draw on.

  The word  async  is there because the function runs  over time : it can stop,
  let a few frames pass, and continue. You do not need to know more about  async  than that.

 Adding a shape
  let ball = view.add(Circle::new().size(160.0).x(-400.0).fill(color!("#68abdf")));

   Circle::new()  starts describing a circle; each  .something(...)  sets how
  it looks at the start — 160 pixels wide, 400 pixels left of the center, light blue.
   view.add(...)
  puts it on screen and gives you back  ball , a handle you use to animate it later.

 The center of the screen is (0, 0). Positive x goes right, positive y goes  down .

 Animating it

  ball.x().to(400.0, 1.0).await;

  Read it as:  take the ball's x, move it to 400 over 1 second, and wait until that is done.

     ball.x()  is the ball's horizontal position. Without an argument it gives you the property;
    with one (like in the builder) it sets the starting value.

     .to(400.0, 1.0)  creates the animation: target value, then duration in seconds.

     .await  plays it and waits. The next line only runs once the ball has arrived.

  So the scene plays its lines from top to bottom, and every  .await  takes time. That is the
  whole model.

      Open this lesson in the playground (link under the preview) and change  1.0  to
       3.0 .

     Add  ball.fill().to(color!("#e13238"), 1.0).await;  before the last line.

      What happens if you remove the  .await  at the end of a line? (The compiler will tell
      you.)

     A scene is an  async fn  with  #[oxframe::scene] .
      view.add(Shape::new()...)  adds a shape and returns a handle.
      handle.property().to(value, seconds).await  animates and waits.

15. Vectors and matrices

  An arrow on a set of axes, a matrix that stretches the whole plane, and the numbers shown beside
  it.

 A vector is an arrow on axes

   axes.vector(1.0, 2.0)  draws an arrow from the origin to the data point (1, 2). It is
  a line, so  .draw_on()  works as in lesson 9, and its tip is two signals:
   v.to(-1.0, 1.0, 1.0)  moves it.

 A matrix moves the plane

   axes.apply_matrix([[2.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]], 1.5)  stretches x by 2. The grid bends and the
  vector follows, because both are drawn through the matrix every frame — the same idea as the ranges
  in lesson 14.

 Showing the numbers

   Matrix::new([[2, 0], [0, 1]])  draws the values in brackets. Each cell is a text node, so
  you can change or color it as the scene goes.

     A shear:  axes.apply_matrix([[1.0, 1.0], [0.0, 1.0]], 1.5) .
     Color a cell:  m.cell(0, 0).fill().to(Accent, 0.3).await .

      axes.vector  draws an arrow; its tip is signals.
      apply_matrix  maps the plane, and everything on the axes follows.

       Matrices, vectors and tables  has row and column frames, matrix
      multiplication step by step, and tables.

 You made it

  That is the whole core of oxframe. From here, browse  all nodes
  and
   effects , open the
   ocean scene  to see everything working together, or
  read
   how oxframe works  inside.

10. Randomness and background tasks

  Lots of things happening on their own, while the main story continues — and still the same video
  every time.

 Random, but repeatable

   random()  gives a number between 0 and 1,  random_range(a, b)  one between
  a and b. They look random, but they come from the project's  seed  ( Project::new(..).seed(7) ), so every run — in the editor, in the final render, on another computer — produces exactly the
  same confetti. Change the seed for a different, again repeatable, result.

  Inside  Custom , use  ctx.rng(seed)  instead.  random()  only
  runs while the scene is stepping, and paint happens after that. A spray that keeps its own motion
  is a
   Particles  node, not a counter in the closure.

  This is a rule worth knowing: oxframe renders the same frames every time. That is why scenes must
  not use the clock or other sources of real randomness.

 Background tasks

   {'spawn(async move  )'}  starts an animation that runs on its own, while the
  scene continues with the next line. Each confetti piece is spawned, falls, and removes itself.
   spawn
  returns a handle you can
   .await  later to wait for the task — here the title waits for the confetti to finish.

     Change the seed.
     Make the pieces fall slower: change  2.0  to  4.0 .

       random()  and  random_range()  are seeded: same video every time.
      Inside  Custom , use  ctx.rng(seed) .

      spawn  runs animations in the background.

 Next

  One scene is not a whole video yet.  Lesson 11  puts several scenes
  in a row and blends them together.

11. Scenes and transitions

  A video is several scenes in a row. One render plays them in order and blends one into the next.

 A project is a list of scenes

  Each  #[oxframe::scene]  function is one scene.  Project::new(..)  takes
  them with  .scene(first()).scene(second())  and plays them in that order. Every scene
  starts with an empty view, so it only holds what it needs.
   oxframe render --scene second
  renders one scene on its own.

 Blend into the next one

   transition(Transition::slide(Dir::Left)).await  at the start of a scene blends it in
  over the one before. The call waits out the blend: nodes added before it are on screen while it
  runs, nodes added after appear when it ends. Without  .duration(..)  the length comes from
  the theme, and the editor can drag it afterwards.

  The built-ins are  fade ,  slide(dir) ,  wipe(dir) ,
   zoom_in  and  zoom_out . The previous scene holds its last frame;
   .overlap()  lets it keep playing. Lesson 13 adds one painted by a shader.

     Change the slide to  Transition::wipe(Dir::Up) .
     Give the fade  .duration(2.0)  and watch the timeline.

     Scenes play in the order you add them with  .scene(..) .

       transition(..)  first thing in a scene blends it in; nodes added before it show during
      the blend.

13. Shaders and effects

  Water, a wet lens, rings and a rising sea: presets that paint pixels, animated like any other
  property.

 A shader is a node

   shaders::waves()  paints water inside its box. Place it like a rectangle, with
   .width(pct(100)) ,  .height(..)  and  .to_edge(Edge::Bottom) .
   .amp()  is the wave height, and it is a signal:  water.amp().to(0.12, 1.0)
  makes the sea grow.  .deep(Accent)  takes its color from the theme.

 Shaders that read the picture

   shaders::lens_drops()  puts drops on the lens over everything drawn before it, so add
  it last and make it  .fullscreen() . Start dry with  .wetness(0.0) ; a
  splash is  lens.wetness().to(1.0, 0.5) .

   node.effect(shaders::ripple())  changes one node's own pixels: rings spread from its
  center. It returns a handle whose  .strength()  you animate. The colors move and the outline
  stays, so use it on water, text or an image.

   Transition::shader(shaders::water_wipe())  is a transition from lesson 11 painted by a shader:
  water rises over the frame and the next scene is under it.

 Make events signals

  A splash at two seconds is a signal change at that moment, not a formula of time. That way the
  editor shows it on the timeline and  oxframe check  sees it. A shader can only read
  finished pixels: inside a fading group or a blur,  check  reports
   input_cycle .
   Rendering video
  has the details.

     A light drizzle:  .wetness(0.3) .
     Taller waves on the line:  water_wipe().wave(0.1) .

     Presets live in  shaders:: ; their parameters are signals.
      lens_drops  goes last;  effect  changes one node.
     Make events signal changes, so the timeline and check see them.

 Next

   Lesson 14  plots functions and data on axes that follow animated
  ranges.

3. Shapes, colors, transforms

  More shapes, outlines, and the properties every shape shares: rotation, scale, color.

 The shapes

   Rect ,  Circle ,  Polygon ,  Star  and
   Line
  are all made the same way:  Shape::new() , then settings.  Rect  has
   .radius()
  for rounded corners,
   Polygon  has  .sides() ,  Line  takes a list of points and can have
  arrows.

 One name, two uses
 This is the pattern you will use everywhere, so it is worth a second look:

   Before adding:  .size(140.0)   sets  the starting size.

    After adding:  .size()   gives you  the size, ready to animate with
     .to(...) .

 Things every shape has

     x ,  y  — position;  rotation  — degrees, clockwise;
     scale
    — a pair, so you can stretch ( Vec2::new(1.4, 0.7) ).

     fill  — the inside color;  stroke  and  line_width  — the outline.

    opacity  — 0 is invisible, 1 is solid.

  Colors are written  color!("#e13238")  (checked when you compile — a typo is an error, not
  a surprise). When a color animates, it blends through perceptually even shades instead of going muddy
  in the middle.

     Give the hexagon an outline:  .stroke(Color::WHITE).line_width(8.0) .
     Animate  star.points()  from 5 to 9.

      All shapes are built the same way and share position, rotation, scale, fill, stroke, opacity.

      .name(value)  sets before adding;  .name()  animates after.

 Themes

  A scene with no colors and no font sizes of its own already looks finished. Nodes take those from
  the project theme:  .fill(Accent) ,  .padding(Md) ,
   .radius(Lg) ,
   Txt::new().display() . Text with no fill uses the theme's text color.

Project::new("explainer").theme(Theme::dark().accent(color!("#68abdf")))

let title = view.add(Txt::new().text("Binary search").display());
let note = view.add(Txt::new().text("O(log n)").caption().fill(Muted));
title.fade_in().await;

  Built-in themes:  dark  (the default),  light ,  midnight ,
   paper  and  vivid .  .accent(color)  rebuilds the palette from
  one brand color and keeps text at a 4.5:1 contrast. The same override can live in
   oxframe.toml  without a recompile:

[theme]
name = "midnight"
accent = "#68abdf"

   fade_in()  and a duration of  Fast ,  Normal  or
   Slow
  use the theme's motion. One  .theme(...)  line changes every token in the video.

 Relative position and frame shape

  Place a node against another node or the safe area instead of counting pixels. The position is
  worked out again every frame, so it follows a neighbor that moves or changes size.  pct(80)  is 80% of the frame width.

let title = view.add(Txt::new().text("Binary search").h1().to_edge(Edge::Top));
let card = view.add(Rect::new().width(pct(80)).height(300.0).fill(Surface));
let label = view.add(Txt::new().text("mid").caption().next_to(card, Side::Bottom));

   align_to(other, Edge::Top)  shares an edge.
   center_in(other)  shares a center.
   to_edge  stops at the safe area: a portrait frame leaves room for a vertical video's
  status bar and buttons.  view.is_portrait()  and
   view.safe_area()  are there when a layout really does have to branch.

  Declare every shape the video should exist in.  oxframe check  looks at each of them,
  and  oxframe render --aspect 9:16  (or
   --aspect all ) exports them.

  Project::new("explainer").aspects([Aspect::Landscape, Aspect::Portrait, Aspect::Square])

 Every shape and all its settings are listed in  All nodes .

8. Signals

  Make one thing follow another automatically — a line that always connects two dots, a label that
  always shows a value.

 Every property is a signal

   a.x()  — what you have been animating — is a  signal : a value that can
  change over time. Besides  .to(...) , signals have  .get()  (read now),
   .set(v)
  (change now) and
   .bind(...) :

  label.x().bind(move || (ax.get() + bx.get()) / 2.0);

  This says:  the label's x is always halfway between the two dots.  Whenever a dot moves, the
  label follows by itself. In the preview only the two dots are animated; the line, the label and its
  text are all bound.

 About  move  and the extra lines

  The formula runs later, every time something changes, so it needs its own copies of the signals it
  reads — that is what  let (ax, bx) = (a.x(), b.x());  before it and  move  in
  front of it are for. Copying a signal is cheap: both copies point to the same value.

  Bound values are computed lazily — only when something needs them for drawing — so binding costs
  almost nothing.

     Bind  b.fill()  so the blue dot turns red when it gets close to the red one.
     Bind the label's  font_size  to the distance.

      Properties are signals:  get ,  set ,  to ,
       bind .

      bind(move || ...)  keeps a value up to date with a formula.

12. Sound and voice

  Sounds start on the frame where the scene starts them, so they stay in sync when the timing
  changes.

 A sound on the beat

   sound("assets/click.wav").play()  starts the file at the current frame.
   .trim(0.0, 0.18)  plays only part of it and  .volume(..)  sets its level. Put
  the call right before the animation it belongs to: if you add a pause earlier in the scene, the click
  moves with the picture.

 A soundtrack under everything

   Project::audio(Audio::track("assets/music.mp3"))  plays under the whole project.
   .duck_under_voice()  makes it quieter while someone speaks.

 A spoken line

   voice("Sound follows the picture").start()  starts a line and returns a handle.
   line.at_word("follows").await  waits for that word, and  line.await  waits
  for the end. Without a speech provider oxframe estimates how long the line takes, which is enough
  to time the picture;  Rendering  shows how to plug in a real
  voice.

     Wait for the word  "picture"  instead of  "follows" .
     Turn the soundtrack up with  .volume(0.8)  and listen to it duck.

      sound(..).play()  starts at the current frame.

       Audio::track(..)  is the soundtrack;  .duck_under_voice()  lowers it.

      line.at_word(..)  times the picture to a word.

5. Text
 Titles, typewriter effects, mixed styles and code.

 Txt

   Txt::new().text("Hello").font_size(96.0).weight(800.0)  is a text shape. Two fonts are
  built in: Inter (default) and JetBrains Mono ( .family(MONO) ). Both include Cyrillic.
  Because the fonts ship with oxframe, your text looks exactly the same on every computer.

 Text animates too

     title.text().to("Hello, text", 1.0)  types the new text like a typewriter.

     .end()  from 0 to 1 reveals the text letter by letter (you will see  end  again
    for shapes in lesson 9).

     title.morph_to("New title", 1.0)  slides letters that both texts share into place and
    fades the rest.

 Mixed styles and code
  Txt::new().rich([span("Mix "), span("bold").bold(), span(" and "), span("color").color(color!("#f5c242"))])

   Code  shows source code with syntax highlighting, and can dim everything except the
  lines you are talking about:  Code::new().code(src).focus(3, 4) . The
   quicksort showcase  uses it heavily.

   code.code().to(next, 1.0)  does not type the new source. Tokens that stay slide to
  their new places, deleted ones fade, and new ones appear.
   insert(line, col, text, seconds) ,
   remove(((line, col), (line, col)), seconds)
  and  replace  edit one spot; lines are counted from 1 and columns from 0.
   .flash()  on that tween lights the inserted text for a moment. A focus on lines that
  move rides with them. The  code steps  example writes
  a function this way.

     Replace the typewriter with  title.morph_to("Hello, world", 1.0).await;
     Make the code bigger with  .font_size(48.0) .

       Txt  for text,  .rich([span(...)])  for mixed styles,  Code  for
      highlighted code.

      Animate  text  (typewriter),  end  (reveal) or call
       morph_to .

2. In order, or all at once

  In lesson 1 things happened one after another. Now you will make several things move at the same
  time.

 One after another

  Two lines, each ending in  .await : the second one starts when the first is finished.

a.x().to(500.0, 0.8).await;
b.x().to(500.0, 0.8).await;

 At the same time:  all

  To play animations together, put them in  all((...))  — note the double parentheses, it
  takes a group of animations — and await that once. It finishes when the  longest  one does.

  all((c.x().to(500.0, 0.8), d.x().to(500.0, 1.6))).await;

 Pauses and waves

   wait_for(0.3).await  simply waits.  stagger(0.1, &wave, |c| ...)  runs the same
  animation on every item of a list, each one starting 0.1 s after the previous — that is the ripple at
  the end of the preview.

  = (0..5).map(|_| view.add(Circle::new())).collect(); -->
  stagger(0.1, &wave, |c| c.y().to(200.0, 0.4)).await;

  For a list of the same animation that should all start at once,  all  takes it
  directly:
   all(wave.iter().map(|c| c.y().to(200.0, 0.4))) .

 Ready-made entrances

  Every shape has a few common moves built in. They take their length and easing from the theme, so
  a whole video stays consistent;  .duration(seconds)  changes one of them.

  title.fade_in().await;
badge.pop_in().await;              // grows from nothing with a small overshoot
card.slide_in(Side::Left).await;   // slides in from the left while fading in
outline.draw_on().await;           // the outline is drawn like with a pen
title.fade_out().duration(0.3).await;

     Wrap the two red squares in  all((...))  so they move together.
     Change the delay in  stagger  to  0.3 .
     Replace the wave's animation with  |c| c.pop_in() .

     Lines with  .await  run in order.
      all((a, b, c)).await  runs them together and waits for all.

       wait_for(seconds)  pauses;  stagger(delay, &list, |x| ...)  ripples through
      a list.

       fade_in ,  pop_in ,  slide_in ,  draw_on  are ready-made
      entrances.

How oxframe works

  You don't need any of this to make animations. Read it if you are curious why scrubbing is
  instant, why renders are reproducible, or how the playground runs Rust in your browser.

 A scene is a coroutine

   #[oxframe::scene]  turns your  async fn  into a future. oxframe polls it
  with a small single-threaded executor:  one poll is one frame . Each awaited
  animation updates its signals and returns "pending" until its time is up, so the code after it
  runs on the right frame.

  Time is virtual: each task keeps its own clock, advanced by exactly one frame per poll. A
   .to(x, 1.0)  that ends between two frames hands the remaining fraction to the next animation,
  so a long chain of steps never drifts from where the timeline says it should be.

 Everything is deterministic

  There is no wall clock and no thread pool in the scene code. Randomness comes from a ChaCha8
  generator seeded by  Project::seed , and every  spawn ed task runs in a
  fixed order. The same code and the same  meta.json  produce the same frames — on your laptop,
  in CI and in the browser.

  That is what makes seeking possible: to show frame 900, oxframe replays the scene from its start
  without drawing anything, which takes milliseconds, and then draws only the frame you asked for.

 Signals

  Every property — position, color, text — is a  Signal . A signal is either a value or a
  function of other signals ( .bind(…) ). Derived signals are lazy: they recompute only
  when read and only if something they depend on changed. Cycles are detected and reported instead
  of hanging.

 From nodes to pixels

    After each frame, the node tree is laid out (flexbox and grid via taffy) and flattened into a
     display list : fills, strokes, images and layers.

    A renderer draws the list.  vello  does it on the GPU through wgpu;
     tiny-skia  on the CPU. Layers with blur, shadow or glow are rasterized only within
    their bounds.

    For video, frames stream to  ffmpeg  through a pipe while the next ones are being drawn.

  Both renderers are checked against the same reference images: the average color difference must
  stay below ΔE 1 in OKLab, which is below what the eye can see.

 The editor and the engine

  Your project compiles into an ordinary binary.  oxframe dev  runs it as a preview
  server; the editor in your browser talks to it over a WebSocket with a small JSON protocol ( seek ,  play ,  set marker …) plus binary frames. When you save, the CLI rebuilds and
  restarts the binary, and the editor reconnects to the same frame.

  Edits to markers, eases and tunables go the other way: the editor sends them, the engine writes
   meta.json  and re-runs the scene — no compilation needed.

 The playground

  The playground sends your code to a compile service that builds it to WebAssembly in a sandbox
  (results are cached by the hash of the source and SDK version). The same engine then runs inside a
  Web Worker in your page. With WebGPU it renders on your GPU through vello into an
   OffscreenCanvas ; without it, it falls back to the CPU renderer. The editor speaks the
  same protocol to the worker as it does to  oxframe dev , so they behave the same.

 Where the code lives

       oxframe-sdk   The Rust crates: core (executor, signals, easing), 2d (nodes, layout), text, render,
        export, preview, protocol.
       oxframe-cli   The  oxframe  command and the embedded editor build.
       oxframe-web   The editor UI, this site, the playground and the compile service.

Icons

  Lucide, Tabler and Simple Icons by name, as nodes you color and animate. Only the icons a scene
  names end up in its binary.

 An icon by name
 Turn on the  icons  feature of  oxframe :

oxframe =

let server = view.add(icon!("lucide:server").size(64.0).color(Accent));
view.add(icon!("tabler:heart-filled"));
view.add(icon!("simple:github").color(Muted));

   icon!  takes the set and the name. The name is the one on the set's site:
   lucide.dev/icons ,
   tabler.io/icons  (add  -filled  for the filled
  variant) and  simpleicons.org  for brand logos. A name that
  does not exist fails to compile and the error lists the closest names, so
   icon!("lucide:arow-right")  suggests  arrow-right .

     Prefix  Set  Icons  License

       lucide:   Lucide, outlines  2,171  ISC
       tabler:   Tabler Icons, outlines and  -filled   6,238  MIT
       simple:   Simple Icons, brand logos  3,466  CC0; the brands are trademarks of their owners

 Size, color and line width

  An icon is a 24 by 24 grid scaled to  .size() , 48 pixels by default. Its color is the
  theme's text color unless you set  .color()  with a color or a theme role. Outline
  icons take  .stroke_width()  on the 24-unit grid, 2 by default; filled icons and logos have
  no lines.

  The handle,  Icon , has  color()  and  stroke_width()  as
  signals, so a whole icon animates at once. It is a node like any other:  fade_in ,
   next_to ,  scale  and layout work on it.  Icon::paths  gives its
  paths one by one, for  draw_on , and  Icon::style  tells an
   IconStyle::Stroke  icon from an  IconStyle::Fill  one.

server.color().to(Danger, 0.3).await;
server.stroke_width().to(3.0, 0.3).await;
for path in server.paths()

 In a flow diagram

   FlowDiagram  puts an icon at the start of a node's card with
   .icon(name, icon!(..)) .  flow.icon(name)  returns its handle.

let flow = view.add(
    FlowDiagram::new()
        .edge("api", "database")
        .icon("api", icon!("lucide:server"))
        .icon("database", icon!("lucide:database")),
);
flow.enter().await;
if let Some(db) = flow.icon("database")

 Any other SVG

   Icon::from_svg(bytes, IconStyle::Stroke)  makes the same node from a 24 by 24 SVG of
  your own. For a logo or an illustration at its own size, use
   the  Svg  node .

 The playground has the feature on, so  icon!  works in a scene there.

Matrices, vectors and tables

  Matrices with cells you can point at, vectors on axes, linear maps that bend the grid, and tables
  whose rows slide into place.

 Matrix

let a = view.add(Matrix::new([[1, 2], [3, 4]]).font_size(64.0));
let row = a.row_frame(0);
row.fade_in().await;
a.cell(0, 1).fill().to(Accent, 0.3).await;

   Matrix::new  takes rows of numbers,  &str  or anything that prints, and
  draws them in square brackets. Every cell is a  Txt :  a.cell(r, c) ,
   a.row(r)  and  a.column(c)  give them, so  .text().set(..)
  changes a value and  .fill()  colors it.  row_frame ,
   column_frame  and  cell_frame  add a rounded outline, hidden until you fade
  it in.  .cell_width(px)  keeps room for values that will be longer than the first ones,
  such as a result filled in step by step;  .font_size(px) ,
   .column_gap(px)  and  .row_gap(px)  set the rest.

 Vectors and linear maps

let axes = view.add(Axes::new().x_range(-4.0..4.0).y_range(-3.0..3.0));
let v = axes.vector(2.0, 1.0);
v.label("v");
axes.apply_matrix([[1.0, 1.0], [0.0, 1.0]], 1.5).await; // a shear
v.to(-1.0, 2.0, 1.0).await;
axes.matrix().to(Mat2::IDENTITY, 1.0).await;

   axes.vector(x, y)  draws an arrow from the origin. Its tip is two signals,
   v.x()  and  v.y() , and  v.to(x, y, seconds)  moves both;
   .label("v")  keeps a label past the tip.

   axes.apply_matrix(m, seconds)  maps the plane through a 2 × 2 matrix, written row by
  row, on top of what was applied before. A transformed grid is drawn over the original one, and
  plots, series, vectors and nodes placed with  axes.place  move with it. The matrix
  itself is
   axes.matrix() , a  Mat2  signal that animates entry by entry; set it back
  to
   Mat2::IDENTITY  to undo.  Mat2::after  multiplies two matrices and
   Mat2::det  gives the determinant. Ticks and labels stay where they were, and placed nodes
  keep their own shape.

 Table

let table = view.add(
    Table::new(["Renderer", "Frame"])
        .row(["skia", "12 ms"])
        .row(["vello", "4 ms"]),
);
table.insert_row(1, ["wgpu", "3 ms"]).await;
table.sort_by_column(1, 0.8).await;
table.row(0).background().fade_in().await;
table.remove_row(2).await;

   Table::new  takes the column titles and  .row(..)  adds rows. Columns fit
  their widest value;  .widths([..])  sets them when rows added later are wider, and
   .font_size(px)  with  .row_height(px)  sizes the text.

  The rows are a list you change while the scene runs.  insert_row  and
   push_row  slide the rows below down and fade the new one in;
   remove_row  fades one out and closes the gap.  sort_by_column  moves every
  row to its sorted place, comparing cells that start with a number ( "12 ms" ) as
  numbers;
   sort_by  takes your own comparison.  table.row(i)  is a
   TableRow  in the current order, with its cells and a hidden background for highlights.

Migrating from Manim

  Manim scenes are Python classes that play animations one  self.play  at a time. oxframe
  scenes are Rust  async fn s that do the same with  .await , with a live
  editor, plots, matrices and morphing built in. This page maps the concepts and ports two scenes.

 How the two models differ

  In Manim,  construct  builds mobjects and hands animations to
   self.play , which renders them before the next line runs. In oxframe each node has
  signals — position, color, the path itself — and  .to(target, seconds).await  animates
  one and waits.  all((…))  is  self.play  with several animations;
   wait_for  is  self.wait .

  Instead of rendering a file and opening it,  oxframe dev  shows the scene in an editor
  you can scrub, and every frame can be reached instantly. The same code runs in the
   browser playground , with no Cairo, LaTeX or Python to install.

  Two habits to drop: Manim measures in units (the frame is about 14.2 wide) with y pointing up;
  oxframe measures in pixels from the center of the frame, with y pointing down. At 1920 × 1080 one
  Manim unit is about 135 px, and  UP  is negative y.

 Concepts side by side

     Manim  oxframe

       class S(Scene): def construct(self)    #[oxframe::scene] async fn s(view: View)
       self.add(m)    view.add(…)
       self.play(Create(m))    m.draw_on().await
       FadeIn ,  FadeOut    m.fade_in().await ,  m.fade_out().await
       Write(text)    text.end().to(1.0, 1.0).await  reveals it letter by letter
       Transform(a, b)    a.data().to(path, 1.0)  for shapes,  t.morph_to("new", 1.0)  for text
       m.animate.shift(RIGHT * 2)    m.x().to(m.x().get() + 270.0, 1.0).await
       self.play(a, b)    all((a, b)).await
       LaggedStart(…, lag_ratio=0.1)    stagger(0.1, &items, |m| m.fade_in()).await
       run_time=2 ,  rate_func=smooth   the seconds argument,  .ease(presets::IN_OUT_CUBIC)
       ValueTracker ,  always_redraw , updaters   Signal::new(…) ,  .bind(move || …)
       Axes ,  axes.plot ,  NumberLine    Axes::new() ,  axes.plot(|x| …) ,  NumberLine::new(…)  —
         charts
       Matrix ,  Table ,  Vector    Matrix::new ,  Table::new ,  axes.vector  —
         matrices
       MovingCameraScene    Camera :  zoom ,  center_on ,
         fit
       ThreeDScene    View3d : lit meshes and glTF models inside a 2D scene
       MathTex ,  Tex   not yet — formulas are planned
       manim -pql scene.py S    oxframe dev  to watch,  oxframe render  for the file

 The same scenes in both

  A circle is drawn, becomes a square and moves right; then a sine wave is drawn on axes and a dot
  rides along it.

     Transform  is a path morph: the shape's  data  signal animates to another path.
    Any two paths morph, with matched start points so they do not twist.

    The  ValueTracker  becomes a  Signal , and  axes.point_on  adds
    a dot that follows it — what  always_redraw  does in Manim.

    Two Manim scene classes become two scenes of one project; they play in order and a
     transition  can join them.

 What does not carry over

     LaTeX.  There is no  MathTex  yet. Formulas are planned; until then, write
    them with rich text and Unicode, or as an SVG made elsewhere.

     Surfaces and 3D plots.  3D covers meshes (cube, sphere, plane, cylinder, glTF) inside
    a 2D frame, not parametric surfaces or 3D axes.

     Python.  The scenes are Rust. They are short and mostly calls like the ones
    above; an agent with the oxframe skill writes them well, and  oxframe check  tells it what
    went wrong.

 Porting a project

   One oxframe scene per Manim scene class, in the same order.

    Turn units into pixels (× 135 at 1920 × 1080) and flip y. Prefer placing with
     next_to ,  to_edge  and  Layout  over coordinates.

    Each  self.play(…)  becomes one  .await , or  all((…)).await  for
    several animations.

   Run  oxframe dev  to compare, then  oxframe check .

  With an agent:  npx skills add oxygenframe/oxframe-sdk  installs the
   manim-to-oxframe skill . Then ask, for example, “Port
  scenes.py to oxframe, one scene per class, and make oxframe check pass”.

Migrating from Motion Canvas

  Motion Canvas is the closest tool to oxframe: scenes are coroutines over signals in both. Porting
  is mostly syntax —  yield*  becomes  .await , refs become handles — and this
  page maps the rest.

 How the two models differ

  A Motion Canvas scene is a TypeScript generator:  yield* circle().x(300, 1)  tweens a
  signal and waits for it. An oxframe scene is a Rust  async fn :
   circle.x().to(300.0, 1.0).await  does the same. Both replay a scene from the start to reach
  any frame, both keep markers and timing edits in a meta file next to the scene, and both have an editor
  with a timeline.

  The difference is around the scene. oxframe is a compiled Rust program:  oxframe render
  writes the video headless, with no editor open, so it runs in CI, and  oxframe check
  reviews every frame for text off screen, overlaps, low contrast and text that is gone too fast.

 Concepts side by side

     Motion Canvas  oxframe

       makeScene2D(function* (view) &#123; … &#125;)    #[oxframe::scene] async fn name(view: View) &#123; … &#125;
       yield* node().x(300, 1)    node.x().to(300.0, 1.0).await
       createRef<Circle>()  and  ref=&#123;…&#125;   the handle that  view.add(…)  returns
       createSignal(0) ,  () => …    Signal::new(0.0) ,  .bind(move || …)
       all(…) ,  chain(…)    all((…)).await ; awaits one after another
       sequence(0.1, …) ,  loop(3, …)    stagger(0.1, &items, …) ,  repeat(3, …)
       yield  a task without  *    spawn(async move &#123; … &#125;)
       waitFor(1) ,  waitUntil('event')    wait_for(1.0) ,  wait_until("event")
       easeInOutCubic ,  easeOutBack    presets::IN_OUT_CUBIC ,  presets::OUT_BACK
       <Layout direction="column" gap=&#123;20&#125;>    Layout::new().column().gap(20.0)
       <Code>  with  edit  and  selection    Code  with  .code().to(next, s) ,  insert ,
         replace ,  focus_lines
       <Line> ,  <Spline> ,  <Ray>    Line  ( .smooth(true) ,  .end_arrow(true) ),
         Path
       <Img> ,  <Video> , the project's audio   Img ,  Video  (feature  video ),
         Audio::track(…)
       slideTransition(Direction.Left)    transition(Transition::slide(Dir::Left)).await
       beginSlide('name')  and the presenter   slide_break().await  and  oxframe present
