       makeProject(&#123;scenes: […]&#125;)    Project::new("name").scene(a()).scene(b())
      rendering from the editor   oxframe render , headless

 The same scene in both
 A circle moves, turns blue while it grows, and a number below counts to 100.

    The refs disappear:  view.add  returns a handle, and handles are  Copy ,
    so they can go into closures and background tasks.

    The computed text  () => count().toFixed(0)  becomes a binding; it is recomputed when
    the signal changes.

     scale(1.5, 1)  sets both axes from one number; in oxframe the target is a
     Vec2 .

 What does not carry over

     LaTeX.  There is no  <Latex>  node yet; formulas are planned.

     Custom TSX components.  A component made of other nodes becomes a Rust function
    that adds them to a  Group ; a node that draws itself uses the
     node API .

     Plugins for the editor.  oxframe's editor is not extensible yet.

 Porting a project

   Port the scenes one by one and keep their names: markers move with the same names.

    Replace  yield*  with  .await , refs with handles, signals with
     Signal ; keep the durations, they are seconds in both.

    Run  oxframe dev  to scrub the result and drag the markers back into place, then
     oxframe check .

  With an agent:  npx skills add oxygenframe/oxframe-sdk  installs the
   motion-canvas-to-oxframe skill . Then ask,
  for example, “Port src/scenes/intro.tsx to oxframe and make oxframe check pass”.

Migrating from Remotion

  Remotion builds every frame from React components. oxframe runs each scene as a Rust
   async fn  on a timeline. This page maps the concepts, ports one composition line by line,
  and lists what has no counterpart yet.

 How the two models differ

  A Remotion component is a function of the frame number:  useCurrentFrame()  and
   interpolate()  compute every value on every frame, and a  <Sequence>
  shifts time for its children. An oxframe scene says what happens in order instead:
   title.opacity().to(1.0, 0.5).await  animates for half a second, then the next line
  runs. Values are signals;  all((…))  runs animations together and  spawn  runs
  one alongside the rest.

  Seeking works the same way in both: oxframe replays the scene up to the frame you ask for, so
  every frame is deterministic and the editor scrubs freely. Rendering needs no browser. oxframe
  draws with its own renderer, on the GPU or with  --cpu  on any machine, and encodes with
  ffmpeg.

 Concepts side by side

     Remotion  oxframe

       <Composition>  with fps, size, duration   Project::new("name").fps(30).size(1920, 1080).scene(main()) ; the length is
        however long the scene runs
       useCurrentFrame()  +  interpolate()    node.opacity().to(1.0, 0.5).await , or a  Signal  animated with
         .to()
       spring()   an ease:  .ease(presets::OUT_BACK)  overshoots,
         oxframe::elastic_out
        bounces
       <Sequence from=&#123;30&#125;>    wait_for(1.0).await  (frames ÷ fps) before it,  spawn  to keep something
        else going, or a scene of its own
       <Series> ,  <TransitionSeries>   scenes in order;  transition(Transition::fade()).await  at the start of the next one
       <AbsoluteFill> , flexbox styles  the  View ;  Layout::new().column().gap(Md)  for rows and columns;
         to_edge ,  next_to
      CSS colors and type  the theme:  Accent ,  Surface ,  .h1() ,
         .radius(Lg)
       <Img> ,  staticFile()    Img::new().file("assets/a.png") ,
         Svg::new().file("assets/logo.svg")
       <OffthreadVideo> ,  <Audio>    Video  (feature  video ),  sound("hit.wav").play() ,
         Audio::track("music.mp3")
       defaultProps , input props  ordinary Rust values; read inputs from a file or the environment before building the
        project
       npx remotion render    oxframe render ;  --jobs  renders 2-second segments in parallel
      Remotion Lambda  a plain CI runner;  --cpu  needs no GPU

 The same scene in both

  A title rises in with a spring, and one second later a line counts up to 100. In Remotion every
  value is computed from the frame; in oxframe the scene plays the same beats in order.

     spring()  becomes an ease with overshoot. It is a curve, not a physics simulation, so
    its length is the one you give it.

     <Sequence from=&#123;30&#125;>  at 30 fps is  wait_for(1.0) . The
    title is still moving then, so its animation runs in  spawn .

    The counter is a  Signal  animated with  .to() ; the text is bound to it
    and follows on every frame.

    The styles become theme roles:  .h1()  and  .body()  for the type, the theme's
    background and text colors for the rest.

 What does not carry over

     HTML and CSS.  oxframe does not render web pages, so DOM layouts, React
    component libraries and CSS effects have to be rebuilt with nodes,  Layout  and the
    theme. Inter and JetBrains Mono are built in; other fonts load with
     oxframe::register_font(include_bytes!(…))  and  .family("Name") .

     npm packages for visuals.  There is no Lottie player. For 3D,
     View3d  covers lit meshes and glTF models, not a full three.js scene.

     Embedding.  There is no published player component for your own web app yet; share
    a rendered video or a playground link instead.

 Porting a project

   List the compositions and the sequences inside each.

    Write one scene per composition, or per large sequence, and turn frame numbers into seconds
    (frames ÷ fps).

    Replace hand-built boxes with  components  where they
    fit:
     TitleCard ,  BulletList ,  LowerThird ,  EndCard .

    Run  oxframe check  until it passes, then compare stills with
     oxframe snapshot --at <seconds> .

  With an agent:  npx skills add oxygenframe/oxframe-sdk  installs the
   remotion-to-oxframe skill  next to the main one. Then
  ask it to port a composition, for example “Port src/Intro.tsx to an oxframe scene and make oxframe check
  pass”.

Migrating from Revideo

  Revideo is a fork of Motion Canvas built for rendering from code: scenes with variables, a render
  function and a player. Its scenes port to oxframe the same way as Motion Canvas scenes; this page
  covers what Revideo adds on top.

 Scenes: the Motion Canvas guide applies

  A Revideo scene is a Motion Canvas generator with a name:  makeScene2D('card', function* …) . Nodes, signals,  all ,  waitFor  and the rest map as in
   Migrating from Motion Canvas :  yield*
  becomes
   .await , refs become the handles  view.add  returns, and the scene's name
  is the name of the  async fn .

 What Revideo adds, in oxframe

     Revideo  oxframe

       useScene().variables.get('name', 'Ada')   ordinary Rust: read the value from the environment or a file in the scene, or build the
        project in  main  from it
       renderVideo(&#123; projectFile, variables, settings &#125;)    NAME=Grace oxframe render --out welcome.mp4 ; a loop in a shell script or CI
        renders one video per input
      rendering in headless Chromium  no browser: oxframe draws frames itself, on the GPU or with  --cpu
      parallel rendering in workers   oxframe render --jobs 8 : 2-second segments in parallel, the same bytes as one
        job
       <Audio> ,  <Video>    sound(…).play() ,  Audio::track(…) ,  Video  (feature
         video )
      the player for your own site  no published player package yet: share the rendered video or a playground link

 The same scene in both
 A welcome title with a name passed in from outside, rendered to a file.

    The variable becomes  std::env::var("NAME")  with a default, so the scene still runs when
    nothing is passed — in the editor and in the playground too.

     renderVideo  becomes the CLI:
     NAME=Grace oxframe render --out welcome.mp4 .

 Porting a project

    Port the scenes as in the  Motion Canvas guide .

    Move each variable into Rust: the environment for one value, a JSON or CSV file for many (read
    it with  std::fs  and  serde ).

    Replace the render script with  oxframe render  in CI;  --cpu  runs on any runner.

   Run  oxframe check  for each input you render.

  With an agent: the
   motion-canvas-to-oxframe skill  covers
  Revideo scenes as well; install it with  npx skills add oxygenframe/oxframe-sdk .

All nodes

  A reference of every node and its properties. If you followed the guide, you already know the
  pattern; this page is for looking things up.

  Builders set initial values;  view.add(builder)  (or  node.add  for
  children) returns a
   Copy  handle whose methods of the same names return signals.

     Node  Builder  Signals

       Rect    .width .height .size .radius    width height radius
       Circle    .size .start_angle .end_angle .pie    size start_angle end_angle  — arcs, pie slices
       Polygon    .sides .size    sides size  — sides animate
       Star    .points .size .inner    points size inner
       Path    .data(BezPath) .svg("M0 0 …")    data  — morphs
       Line    .points .smooth .closed .start_arrow .end_arrow    points arrow_size
       Txt    .text .rich([span(..)]) .font_size .weight .family .italic .align .max_width    text spans font_size weight ,  morph_to
       Code    .code .language .theme .focus(a, b) .dim    font_size focus dim ,  code().to  (a token diff),
         insert ,  remove ,  replace ,  focus_lines
       Img    .src(include_bytes!(..)) .file(path) .width .height    width height
       Svg    .src(include_bytes!(..)) .file(path) .width .height    width height ,  find("id") ,  paths()
       Layout    .row .column .wrap .grid(n) .gap .padding .align .justify .width .height    gap padding width height radius
       Grid    .width .height .spacing    width height spacing
       Group   —  —
       Custom    .new(|ctx, t| …) .size .fullscreen   paints each frame;  ctx.rng(seed) ,  ctx.time()
       Particles    .seed .gravity .life .speed .radius .toward_camera    gravity ,  burst(origin, count)
        Camera     .zoom    zoom  (and  x y rotation ),  center_on fit reset

  Every node has  x y rotation scale opacity fill stroke line_width start end , the paint
  and compositing properties described in  Effects , and the flex
  item properties  grow shrink basis margin align_self .  start / end
  trim outlines — animate  end  from 0 to 1 to draw a shape on (on text it reveals glyph by
  glyph).

   Svg  reads a whole file and turns it into those nodes: groups stay groups, shapes
  become  Path s (so  data  still morphs), and embedded PNG or JPEG images
  become  Img .  find("id")  is the element with that id.
   paths()  is every contour in paint order. Filters, masks and clip paths are skipped
  with a warning.  Svg::new().width()  and  .height()  take pixels or
   pct()  of the parent, read when the node is added; set one and the other keeps the drawing's
  aspect.

 Video

   Video::new().file("assets/demo.mp4")  shows a clip as a node: a screen recording in a
  laptop frame, a product demo next to a diagram. Turn on the  video  feature of
   oxframe ; clips are decoded with ffmpeg, which  oxframe render  already
  needs. Size it like an image with  .width(pct(70))  — the height follows the clip —
  round it with  .radius(24.0) , and add effects or put it under a camera like any node.

let demo = view.add(Video::new().file("assets/demo.mp4").width(pct(70)).radius(24.0));
demo.play();
wait_for(2.0).await;
demo.playback_rate().to(0.25, 0.5).await;   // slow motion

   demo.play()  returns at once and the clip plays alongside the scene;
   demo.pause()  holds the frame and  demo.seek(2.0)  jumps.
   demo.playback_rate()  and  demo.time()  are signals, so
   demo.playback_rate().to(0.25, 0.5)  eases into slow motion and animating
   time  scrubs. The frame shown is a function of the scene's time, so a render and a seek
  in the editor show the same frame. MP4 (H.264), WebM (VP9, with alpha) and ProRes 4444 (with alpha)
  are read.

  The clip's sound goes into the mix while it plays at rate 1;  .muted(true)  leaves it
  out. A clip that cannot be opened draws a dark box and fails  oxframe check  with
   video_unavailable . The browser playground cannot read your files, so there a video is
  always that box;  oxframe dev  plays it.

 Your own geometry

   Custom::new(|ctx, t| {' '})  paints the frame itself.
   ctx.line ,  ctx.circle ,  ctx.rect  and  ctx.path
  take
   .fill  or  .stroke . Take numbers from  t  and
   ctx.rng(seed) . The closure runs after the scene step, so  random()  is not
  available there, and a counter closed over from outside fails  check  as
   nondeterministic .

   Particles  keeps a seeded spray:  .seed(7).gravity(900.0).toward_camera()
  and  burst(origin, count).await . Seeking back replays from a checkpoint, so the dots
  match.  toward_camera  only scales them.

 Shapes and morphing

  Tweening  Path::data  between any two paths aligns them first (segment counts, start points,
  winding), so shapes morph without twisting.

 Layout

   Layout  is real flexbox (and CSS grid with  .grid(columns) ), computed by
  taffy. Children take
   .grow ,  .shrink ,  .basis ,  .margin  and
   .align_self ;
   LayoutAlign::Stretch  resizes rects, images and nested layouts. Layout properties are signals:
  animate the width or the gap and everything re-flows.

 Text

  Inter and JetBrains Mono are embedded (OFL), so text renders identically everywhere. Strings tween
  like a typewriter.

 Rich text, code and morphing

Txt::new().rich([span("Signals are "), span("lazy").bold().color(color!("#f5c242"))])
Code::new().language("rust").code(src).focus(3, 4)   // code.focus_lines(5, 5, 0.4).await moves it
code.code().to(next, 1.0).await                       // tokens slide; not a typewriter
code.insert(3, 0, "    let y = x * 2;\n", 0.6).flash().await
code.remove(((5, 0), (6, 0)), 0.5).await              // lines from 1, columns from 0
word.morph_to("frame", 1.0).await                    // shared letters travel, the others fade

  Highlighting covers Rust, JS/TS, Python, JSON, TOML and shell, with One Dark and One Light themes.

Presentations

  The same scenes that render to a video become a talk: the presentation stops where you mark it and
  waits for the next click.

 Stops and notes

#[oxframe::scene]
pub async fn opening(view: View) {
    notes("Introduce yourself.");
    let title = view.add(TitleCard::new("Video as code"));
    title.enter().await;
    wait_for(1.5).await;
    slide_break().await;

    notes("Each point appears on the next click.");
    let points = view.add(BulletList::new(["Scenes are async Rust", "Every value is a signal"]));
    points.enter().await;
    for _ in 0..2
}

   slide_break().await  marks a stop. A render plays straight through it, so the project
  is still a video; the presentation pauses there. The last frame of every scene is a stop too, and
  a break at the very end of a scene is the same stop.  notes("…")  are speaker notes for the
  part that ends at the next stop; several calls before one stop are joined.

  Hold before each break with  wait_for . The video plays straight through the stops, and
  without a hold the text is gone before anyone reads it —  oxframe check  reports that
  as
   too_fast . In the presentation the hold is a still frame just before the stop, so
  nobody sees it.

 Presenting
  oxframe present

   oxframe present  builds the project and opens it full screen in the browser, without the
  editor around it. → , space, Page Down and a click go to the next stop: the scene plays up to it and
  stops. Pressed while it plays, the next key jumps straight to the stop. ← and Page Up go back one stop,
  Home to the start. Slide clickers send these keys, so they work as they are. F toggles full screen.

  N opens the presenter window: the notes for the current part and the next one, the stop number and
  a timer. Put it on your laptop screen and the presentation on the projector; its keys and buttons
  move the presentation as well. Going back is safe even with  spawn  and random values: the
  state of a scene depends only on its frame.

  The presentation is the live project: saving a source file rebuilds it, as in
   oxframe dev . The playground on this site plays the scenes straight through.

 Slides as a PDF
  oxframe render --slides talk.pdf

   render --slides talk.pdf  writes one page per stop, the frame the presentation shows
  there, for handouts or a fallback. It needs no ffmpeg;  --size  and  --cpu
  work as for a video.

Rendering video

  When the animation looks right in the editor, one command turns it into a video file.

  oxframe render

  That's it: the project is built in release mode and every frame goes to  out/<project>.mp4 . You need  ffmpeg  installed for video formats; PNG frames
  work without it.

 Common recipes

oxframe render --out film.webm             # VP9 with transparency
oxframe render --format prores --out a.mov # ProRes 4444 with transparency, for video editors
oxframe render --format png --out frames/  # one PNG per frame
oxframe render --size 3840x2160            # 4K
oxframe render --scene outro               # just one scene
oxframe render --range 1..3                # seconds 1 to 3
oxframe render --gpu                       # draw on the GPU (vello); the CPU is the default
oxframe render --jobs 4                    # four segments at once

  Need just one still?  oxframe snapshot --at 2.5  writes a PNG of that moment — no ffmpeg,
  no full render.

 Transitions

  A scene can open by blending in over the one before it. The call waits out the blend, so nodes
  added before it are on screen while it runs and nodes added after appear when it finishes. The
  length comes from the theme unless you set one, and the editor can drag it afterwards.

#[oxframe::scene]
async fn outro(view: View)

   fade ,  slide(Dir::Left)  ( Right ,  Up ,
   Down ),  wipe(dir) ,  zoom_in  and  zoom_out  are
  built in.  .ease(...)  changes the curve,  .overlap()  lets the previous
  scene keep playing instead of holding its last frame, and  Transition::custom(|t| ...)
  places the two layers itself with opacity, offset, scale and a wipe.
   Transition::shader(shaders::water_wipe())  raises a wavy waterline over the frame;
  below it is the next scene, rippled near the line, and  .wave()  sets the wave height
  (see  shaders that read pixels ). The first scene has
  nothing to blend from, so the call does nothing there.

   oxframe render  includes every transition.  oxframe render --scene outro
  draws that scene on its own, without the blend into it.  oxframe check  puts a frame
  from each blend on the storyboard, and  oxframe inspect  reports the type and progress. The
  same blend keeps its alpha on a transparent background, in 16:9, 9:16 and 1:1.

 Shaders

   shaders::waves()  is a node: a crest of foam over deeper water, painted inside its
  box.
   .amp()  is the height of that crest and a signal, so it can move.
   .deep()  and  .foam()  take a color or a theme role such as
   Accent . The node has no children. A title goes on the view, above the water.

let sea = view.add(shaders::waves().amp(0.05).deep(Accent).foam(Surface)
    .width(pct(100)).height(pct(40)).to_edge(Edge::Bottom));
sea.amp().to(0.12, 1.2).await;

  The preset is rasterized first and then drawn by the CPU or the GPU, so a check with no GPU still
  shows it. Draft checks paint the layer at half resolution. That does not move the box or change
  the timing.

  Your own shader is WGSL. It defines  struct Params , the uniform  p , and
   fn shade . oxframe adds  ox  (time, frame, resolution, the box size, seed,
  the camera matrix, and progress) and  ShadeIn  (uv, local, world, and screen).
   Shader::source  keeps the text in the scene.
   Shader::file  reads a  .wgsl  file on every draw, so saving it updates the
  picture without a rebuild.  .uniform()  sets a number. A name or a type that is not in
   Params  fails the check, and the message lists the fields. WGSL that does not compile
  fails it too, with the line in your source. A custom  shade  is type-checked on every draw.
  The waves preset is what gets painted.

 Shaders that read pixels

  Three presets work on what is already drawn: drops on the lens, rings on a node, and water that
  rises into the next scene.

#[oxframe::scene]
async fn sea(view: View)

#[oxframe::scene]
async fn shore(view: View)

   shaders::lens_drops()  bends everything drawn before it, inside its box, so add it
  last and make it  .fullscreen() .  .wetness()  runs from 0 (dry) to 1 and is
  a signal:  lens.wetness().to(1.0, 0.4)  is a splash.  .seed()  places the
  drops and  .drop_size()  scales them.  .input("scene", Input::frame())
  names what the shader reads, and outside a layer  Input::backdrop()  is the same thing.

   Node::effect  runs a shader on one node's pixels, children included, and returns an
   Effect .  shaders::ripple()  sends rings out from the node's center;
   .strength()  and  .speed()  are signals. The colors move and the outline stays,
  so use it on water, text, a gradient or an image: a flat fill shows no rings. A node has one effect.

  A shader can only read finished pixels.  lens_drops  or an effect inside a group with
  opacity below 1, a blur, a clip, a blend, a shadow or another effect fails
   oxframe check  with  input_cycle , and the shader is skipped. Put the
  effect on that group instead.  oxframe inspect --graph  lists these shaders as
   effect  passes, and a  Shader  handle works wherever a  Node
  does, for example in  Camera::center_on .

  Not there yet:  Input::node  (another node as a texture),  Input::image
  (a texture file),  .offscreen() , and running your own  shade , which is
  still only checked.

 Sound

  A soundtrack plays for the whole video.  Project::audio("music.mp3")  still works, and
  it is the same as  Audio::track :

Project::new("explainer")
    .audio(Audio::track("assets/music.mp3").duck_under_voice().volume(0.8))
    .scene(intro())

   .duck_under_voice()  lowers the music while a sound marked  .priority()  is
  playing.  .volume() ,  .fade_in()  and  .fade_out()  shape the
  track.  .master_fade()  fades the whole mix, including the effects.

   sound("click.wav")  starts at the current frame.  .play()  does not wait.
  Awaiting the sound waits until it ends, and  .trim()  plays a slice of the file (that slice
  is also how long the wait is):

sound("assets/whoosh.wav").volume(0.6).fade_in(0.05).play();
sound("assets/click.wav").trim(0.0, 0.2).priority().await;

  Effects show up as clips on the timeline and play with the picture, including after a seek. The
  mix is written before ffmpeg encodes it, so two renders of the same scene match.
   --no-audio  leaves the soundtrack and the effects out.  --range  keeps only
  the part of them that falls inside that span. Drag the waveform to shift the soundtrack; the
  offset is saved in  meta.json .

 Voice

   voice("one two").start()  speaks the line and keeps going.  .at_word()
  waits until that word. Awaiting the line waits until the end. A line is  .priority() ,
  so it ducks a soundtrack built with  .duck_under_voice() .

let line = voice("First draw a square, then rotate it").start();
line.at_word("square").await;
square.draw_on().await;
line.at_word("rotate").await;
square.rotation().to(90.0, 0.8).await;
line.await;

  oxframe does not call a speech service itself. To get real audio, implement
   TtsProvider  and pass it to  Project::tts .  synthesize
  receives the line and the voice name and returns mono  i16  samples plus one
   TimedWord  per word.  .at_word()  waits on those times, not on a guess. The
  key stays inside the provider, read from the environment.  speak  below is your function:
  the HTTP call and the decode.

  Result , Vec ), String>   -->

use oxframe:: ;

struct ElevenLabs;

impl TtsProvider for ElevenLabs {
    fn id(&self) -> &str

    fn synthesize(&self, req: &TtsRequest) -> Result  {
        let key = std::env::var("ELEVENLABS_API_KEY")
            .map_err(|_| "set ELEVENLABS_API_KEY".to_string())?;
        // Send req.text and req.voice to ElevenLabs with key.
        // Decode the body into mono i16 samples and one TimedWord per word.
        let (rate, samples, words) = speak(&key, req.voice, req.text)?;
        Ok(Synthesis  )
    }
}

Project::new("explainer")
    .tts(ElevenLabs)
    .speaker("Rachel")
    .audio(Audio::track("assets/music.mp3").duck_under_voice())
    .scene(intro())

  The first render calls  synthesize  and saves  tts/&#123;hash&#125;.wav  and
   tts/&#123;hash&#125;.json . The next render plays that file. Commit the folder to
  render in CI without a key. A missing key or a failed call does not fail the scene: oxframe
  estimates the length (2.5 words per second, at least 0.3s) and there is no speech audio. An
  estimate is not cached. With no provider, a committed cache is still used when the text and voice
  match. The playground always estimates.

   oxframe render --subtitles out.srt  writes the lines. A path ending in
   .vtt
  writes WebVTT.  --no-audio  still writes them, and  --range  shifts the cues into
  that part of the video. A line that runs past the scene is an error; two lines that overlap are a warning.

 Transparent backgrounds

  Make the background transparent with  .background(Color::TRANSPARENT)  on the project
  and render to  webm ,  prores  or  png : those keep the alpha
  channel, so you can lay the animation over footage in a video editor. MP4 (H.264) has no
  transparency.

 Parallel rendering

  A video longer than two seconds renders in 2-second segments, several at once: each one runs in
  its own process, is encoded on its own, and the segments are joined without encoding them again.
  The soundtrack is added once at the end.  --jobs 4  sets how many run at a time; the default
  is one per core, at most eight.

  The segments are the same whatever  --jobs  is, so  --jobs 1  and
   --jobs 8  write the same bytes: a render on your laptop and one in CI match. Scenes
  that take long to draw gain the most — a 7-second 3D scene on 8 cores renders 2.7 times faster —
  while a short or simple one gains little, because every segment first runs the scene up to where
  it starts. Each process holds one frame at a time, so memory does not grow with the length of the
  video. A PNG sequence is split the same way. A tool of your own that encodes segments can join
  them the same way with  oxframe_export::concat .

 GPU or CPU?

  Frames are drawn on the CPU (tiny-skia) by default. It is faster than the GPU on every scene we
  benchmark, and it needs no graphics driver, so CI and servers just work. Pass
   --gpu  to  oxframe render ,  oxframe dev  or
   oxframe present  to draw with vello; it falls back to the CPU when no GPU is
  available. Before 0.21 the GPU was the default and  --cpu  opted out;
   --cpu
  still works and wins over  --gpu . Vector scenes match across the two: they pass the
  same reference-frame tests within a color difference of ΔE 1, which you cannot see. The CPU
  renderer is also byte-for-byte identical between runs, which is what you want in automated tests.
  A  shaders::waves()  node is painted into an image before either backend, so the two
  show the same crest. The same goes for
   lens_drops ,  ripple  and  water_wipe : both renderers draw the
  vectors, and the shader runs on those pixels on the CPU. A layer whose vectors did not change is
  reused on the next frame. A scene with no effects is one vector pass;
   oxframe inspect --graph  lists the passes.

 In a container or CI

   ghcr.io/oxygenframe/oxframe  has the oxframe command, Rust and ffmpeg, with the SDK
  already compiled, so a project's first  oxframe check  or  oxframe render
  inside it takes seconds instead of compiling the engine. Use the tag of your project's SDK version:

docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/work" ghcr.io/oxygenframe/oxframe:$  oxframe render

 In GitHub Actions, run the job in it:

jobs:
  video:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    container: ghcr.io/oxygenframe/oxframe:$
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: oxframe check
      - run: oxframe render

 In the browser

  The playground can export MP4 too (the  Export  button). It encodes with your browser's
  WebCodecs, so it works offline but is limited to what the browser supports — use the CLI for ProRes,
  4K or long videos.

Markers, eases, tunables

  The full story behind  lesson 7 : values that live outside
  your code so you can adjust them in the editor.

 The three kinds

wait_until("beat").await;                    // marker: a point on the timeline
x.to(300.0, 1.0).ease(ease!("slide")).await;   // named ease: a curve you can bend
let speed = tune!("speed", 1.4);               // tunable: a number with a slider

        Marker

         wait_until(name)  pauses the current task until the marker's time. The first time
        it runs, the marker is placed where the code reached it — so nothing changes until you drag it.

        Ease

         ease!(name)  is a cubic Bézier curve, like CSS  cubic-bezier() . It
        starts as a smooth in-out; edit it in the curve editor or pick a preset there.

        Tunable

         tune!(name, default)  returns a number. Use it for anything you want to dial in by
        eye: sizes, speeds, counts, delays.

 The meta file

  Each scene has a  src/<scene>.meta.json  next to its source. Code provides defaults;
  the file stores what you changed. Names missing from the file are added with their defaults the first
  time the scene runs.

{
  "eases":  ,
  "markers":  ,
  "tunables":  ,
  "version": 1
}

  Keys are sorted and unknown keys are preserved, so the file is safe to edit by hand and gives
  clean diffs. Commit it together with the code.

 Good to know

    Changing a value in the editor does  not  recompile — the preview updates instantly.

   Names are per scene. Two scenes can each have their own  "speed" .

    Renaming a marker in code creates a new one at its default position; the old entry stays in the
    file until you delete it.

    oxframe check  validates all meta files.

 A bigger example

  The player above is that chart. It uses a marker to sync the bars with a beat and named eases for
  their motion.

Troubleshooting

  The messages people meet on a first install or a first render, what they mean, and the fix. Each
  heading is the text you see.

 Start with oxframe doctor

   oxframe doctor  checks Rust, the C linker, ffmpeg and the project's SDK version, and prints
  the fix for whatever is missing on your system. Most of the problems below show up there first.

 version `GLIBC_2.39' not found (required by oxframe)

  The prebuilt Linux binary of oxframe-cli 0.21.0 needs a newer glibc than Debian 12 or Ubuntu 22.04
  have. From 0.22.0 the binaries run with glibc 2.34 or newer: install again with the installer, or
  build the command on your machine with  cargo install oxframe-cli .

 linker `cc` not found

  Rust compiles your scene and then links it with the system C toolchain. A machine that has never
  built C or Rust code has none. Install it once:

sudo apt install build-essential   # Debian, Ubuntu
sudo dnf install gcc               # Fedora
sudo pacman -S base-devel          # Arch
xcode-select --install             # macOS

  On Windows the error is  linker `link.exe` not found : install the Visual Studio Build
  Tools with the  Desktop development with C++  workload (rustup offers it when you install
  Rust), then open a new terminal.

 cannot be built because it requires rustc 1.95 or newer
 Your Rust is older than the SDK needs. Update it:
  rustup update stable

 ffmpeg was not found in PATH

   oxframe render  hands frames to ffmpeg to make MP4, WebM or ProRes. Install it, or
  point oxframe at a copy with  ffmpeg = "/path/to/ffmpeg"  under  [render]
  in
   oxframe.toml :

sudo apt install ffmpeg         # Linux (or dnf / pacman)
brew install ffmpeg             # macOS
winget install Gyan.FFmpeg      # Windows, then open a new terminal

  Everything else works without it:  oxframe dev ,  oxframe check ,
   oxframe snapshot  and  oxframe render --format png .

 cannot listen on 127.0.0.1:3000 (another `oxframe dev`? use --port)

  The editor's port is taken, usually by an  oxframe dev  still running in another
  terminal. Stop that one, or start this one elsewhere:  oxframe dev --port 3001 .

 protocol versions differ

   oxframe check  stops with exit code 3 when the  oxframe  command and the project's
  SDK speak different editor protocols. Install the newest command, then move the project to it:

cargo install oxframe-cli
oxframe upgrade

  See  Versions and upgrades  for what an upgrade changes.

 build failed; the previous version keeps running

  In  oxframe dev  this is not a crash. Your last save does not compile, so the editor
  keeps showing the last version that did. The compiler error is in the terminal; fix it and save,
  and the editor picks the new build up. A scene that panics again and again stops with
   project keeps crashing; fix the code and save to retry ; the next save starts it again.

 No GPU, or a server or CI runner

  Nothing to do: frames are drawn on the CPU by default, so oxframe needs no graphics driver.
   --gpu  asks for vello on Vulkan, Metal or DirectX 12 and falls back to the CPU when the
  machine has no usable adapter.

 WSL

  Install Rust and ffmpeg inside the Linux distribution, not on Windows. If  oxframe dev
  cannot open a browser, copy the address it prints, token included, into the browser on Windows; WSL
  2 forwards  127.0.0.1  to Windows by default. Keep projects in the Linux file system ( ~/… , not  /mnt/c/… ): builds and file watching are much faster there.

 The disk fills up

  Rust keeps each project's build cache in  target/ , a few gigabytes per project. Run
   cargo clean  in a project you are not working on to get the space back; the next build starts
  from scratch.

 Works locally, not in the playground

  The browser playground builds with a fixed set of features. Video clips ( video ) and
  formulas ( math ) are not in it; scenes that use them run with  oxframe dev  on
  your machine.

 Still stuck

  Open an issue on
   GitHub  with the
  command, its full output,  oxframe --version  and your system. Add
   -v  to the command for detailed logs.

Versions and upgrades

  oxframe is before 1.0, so its API still changes. Here is how versions are numbered, how often they
  come out, and how to move a project from one to the next.

 How versions are numbered

  The SDK crates and the  oxframe  command are released together under one version. Before
  1.0, a release that breaks your code raises the minor number (0.20 → 0.21); a release that only adds
  or fixes something raises the patch number (0.21.0 → 0.21.1).

     Release  What it may do  Your code

      0.21.0 → 0.21.1  Fix bugs, add new API  Builds unchanged
      0.20.x → 0.21.0  Change or remove API, change a default  May need edits; the changelog shows them

 How often

  About once a week. Breaking changes wait for the next minor release and come out together, so you
  update your scenes once instead of after every change. An urgent fix ships on its own as a patch
  release. Every release has its own section in the  changelog , with a short
  video of what is new.

 Pin the version

   oxframe init  pins the exact SDK version in  Cargo.toml , so a new release
  never changes a project behind your back:

[dependencies]
oxframe = "=0.21.0"

  Keep the  = . With a plain  "0.21" , Cargo may pick a newer patch the next
  time the lock file is refreshed.

 Upgrade a project

cargo install oxframe-cli   # the newest oxframe command
cd my-video
oxframe upgrade             # pin this command's SDK, refresh Cargo.lock and the agent files
oxframe check               # build, then look at what changed

   oxframe upgrade  moves the project to the SDK version the installed command is made
  for, updates  Cargo.lock , and refreshes  AGENTS.md  and the agent skill so
  an AI agent writes code for the new version. Then read the changelog sections between your old
  version and the new one. A breaking change is listed under  Changed  or
   Breaking  with a before → after example, which is usually the whole edit.

 Docs for your version

  These docs describe the newest release. The version menu at the top of the docs switches to the
  pages of an older one, kept as they were:  /docs/0.20.5/… ,  /docs/0.19.0/…
  and so on. The API reference on docs.rs is per version too. For an AI agent, point it at the docs of
  the version the project pins:  https://oxframe.dev/docs/0.20.5/llms.txt  for an older
  project,  /llms.txt  for the newest.
